entry.title: HCENC: A Method for Designing an Efficient Committing Accordion Mode Beyond the Birthday Bound from a Block Cipher
entry.summary: HCENC: How to Design an Efficient Committing Beyond-Birthday-Bound Accordion from a Block Cipher with n-Bit Blocks and Keys IACR ePrint · Nov 27, 2026This paper introduces HCENC, a generalization of HCTR for encrypting variable-length inputs, built from a block cipher with n-bit blocks and keys, an n-bit AXU hash function, and the keystream generator of CENC. In the ideal-cipher model, the authors prove it is a strong tweakable pseudorandom permutation up to about 2^n/w blocks. They also analyze key commitment, showing that the block cipher alone keeps CMT-1 at the birthday bound, and report 116-bit CMT-1 and CMT-4 security for concrete AES-based instantiations. ★★★★ Notable: The authors construct a beyond-birthday-bound committing accordion from an n-bit block cipher, proving strong tweakable PRP security in the ideal-cipher model with small per-message overhead and machi

entry.title: Beyond Stepwise Transformation: A MILP Model for Smaller Linear Layer Circuits
entry.summary: Beyond Stepwise Transformation: MILP Model for Low-Area Implementations of Linear Layers IACR ePrint · Nov 27, 2026This paper studies low-area implementations of linear layers used in lightweight symmetric-key cryptography. The authors argue that an existing stepwise method can restrict the search space, and they propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that starts from an XOR2 circuit and jointly selects two-, three-, and four-input XOR gates. For AES MixColumns in the STM 130 nm library, the model yields 236.99 GE, improving on the previous 243 GE. On more than 5000 32×32 MDS matrices, the authors report average area reductions of up to about 28% over initial XOR2 circuits and about 8% over previous stepwise multi-input implementations.

entry.title: Hidden Messages to Many Groups: Public-Key Encryption with Anamorphic Broadcast
entry.summary: Anamorphism Beyond One-To-One Messaging: PKE with Public-Key Anamorphic Broadcast Encryption IACR ePrint · Nov 25, 2026This paper extends Anamorphic Cryptography from one-to-one communication to one-to-many broadcast settings. It presents the first lattice-based anonymous multi-channel broadcast encryption scheme and uses it to add a public-key anamorphic broadcast mode to the Dual Regev encryption scheme. The security claims are proven in the random oracle model under the k-LWE assumption.

entry.title: One-bit-per-gate distributed garbling and constant-round malicious-secure MPC
entry.summary: One-Bit-per-Gate Distributed Garbling and Constant-Round Malicious MPC IACR ePrint · Nov 26, 2026This paper presents a distributed garbling protocol in which several mutually distrustful parties jointly generate a garbled circuit that keeps the privacy and authenticity of a single trusted garbler as long as one party is honest. Under Ring-LWE and constant-locality PRG assumptions, each garbler communicates an amortized one bit per gate. The protocol uses constant rounds and remains secure against a malicious adversary corrupting all but one garbler. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report a distributed garbling protocol with about one bit per gate per garbler, constant rounds, and malicious security under Ring-LWE and constant-locality PRG assumptions.

entry.title: DEEP Revisited: Proximity Gaps Up to List-Decoding Radius Using Out-of-Domain Samples
entry.summary: DEEP Revisited: Proximity Gaps up to List-Decoding Radius via Out-of-Domain Samples IACR ePrint · Nov 26, 2026This paper revisits the use of out-of-domain samples for proximity gaps, a technique first introduced in DEEP-FRI. Over sufficiently large fields, multiple such samples give proximity-gap guarantees for linear codes at any list-decodable radius below the minimum distance. For general linear codes, the guarantee extends from the one-and-a-half Johnson bound to the full Johnson bound using a constant number of samples. For Reed-Solomon codes, the bounds hold beyond the Johnson radius even when the list size is much larger than 2^λ. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors extend out-of-domain sample proximity gaps from the one-and-a-half Johnson bound to the full Johnson bound, giving proofs and error and sample-count analyses relevant to hash-based SNARK s

entry.title: A Faster Provable Algorithm for Random Modular Subset Sum
entry.summary: Faster Provable Algorithm For Random Modular Subset Sum IACR ePrint · Nov 26, 2026This paper studies the random modular subset sum problem, where coefficients are drawn uniformly modulo Q and the target is the inner product with a hidden binary vector. It focuses on the balanced density-one case with Q=2^n and Hamming weight n/2. The authors present a classical randomized algorithm that, for sufficiently large n, finds a solution with overwhelming probability using at most 2^0.2614n bit operations and 2^0.2373n bits of space, without heuristic assumptions. This improves on the previously reported best classical time bound of 2^0.283n. ★★★★ Notable: The authors improve the classical time bound for balanced density-one random modular subset sum from 2^0.283n to 2^0.2614n, without heuristic assumptions, also giving a space bound.

entry.title: Classical key agreement with near-quadratic quantum security
entry.summary: Classical Key Agreement with Near-Quadratic Quantum Security IACR ePrint · Nov 26, 2026The paper presents two classical key-establishment protocols in the random oracle query model: a two-message protocol and a three-message protocol with perfect agreement. Honest parties make about Õ(N) classical oracle queries, while any quantum eavesdropper with constant success probability needs Õ(N²) quantum queries to recover the key. The result is tight up to logarithmic factors, since the quadratic classical attack of Barak and Mahmoody also applies in this setting. ★★★★ Notable: The authors present two classical key agreement protocols where honest parties use near-linear queries while quantum eavesdroppers need near-quadratic queries, tight up to logarithmic factors.

entry.title: NP-completeness of worst-case (2,1) quasi-cyclic syndrome decoding
entry.summary: On the NP-Completeness of Worst-Case (2,1)-Quasi-Cyclic Syndrome Decoding IACR ePrint · Nov 26, 2026This paper studies the worst-case (2,1) quasi-cyclic syndrome decoding problem over the ring F2[X]/(X^n-1), asking whether polynomials x and y exist with x+hy=s and equal block weights w. The authors prove the problem is NP-complete in the low-weight regime w<√n via a polynomial-time reduction from 3-Dimensional Matching. The same reduction also covers a relaxed variant requiring only weights at most w. The result is further extended to prime block lengths and general fixed (a,b)-QCSD instances. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report NP-completeness of worst-case (2,1)-QCSD via a polynomial reduction from 3DM, extending to prime lengths and general (a,b) instances.

entry.title: Fault attacks that recover secret keys from three post-quantum signature schemes
entry.summary: Faulting the Proof: Key Recovery Attacks on MQOM, SDitH and FAEST IACR ePrint · Nov 26, 2026This paper examines how well the MQOM, SDitH and FAEST signature schemes resist faults during computation of their proof of key knowledge. The authors exploit a value that is omitted from signatures but still bound through a hash, using it to test key guesses from faulty signatures. Clock-glitch experiments on an STM32F405 microcontroller recover the full secret key of all three schemes. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show an omitted value bound by a hash enables fault-based key guessing, correcting prior MQOM analysis; they report full key recovery on all three schemes via clock glitches on an STM32F40

entry.title: Recovering the full structure of linearized Reed–Solomon codes from a generator matrix
entry.summary: Full Structure Recovery of Linearized Reed–Solomon Codes IACR ePrint · Nov 26, 2026This paper studies linearized Reed–Solomon (LRS) codes, which are considered for post-quantum code-based cryptography. The authors present a polynomial-time procedure that recovers the full structure of an LRS code using only an arbitrary generator matrix. The results show that LRS codes, like Hamming and rank-metric codes, cannot be used as they are for McEliece-like encryption. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a polynomial-time full structure recovery of LRS codes from an arbitrary generator matrix, combining Overbeck-type attacks with shortening, implying LRS codes are unsuitable for Mc

entry.title: Parity leakage and sparse-mask sampling in distorted McEliece pseudorandom codes
entry.summary: Parity Leakage and Sparse-Mask Sampling in Distorted-McEliece Pseudorandom Codes IACR ePrint · Nov 27, 2026The paper examines the binary public-key pseudorandom codes proposed by Dyseryn, Francati and Venturi, showing that with the full support their public key can be distinguished from a uniform matrix by computing parities, which refutes their Distorted McEliece Public Key assumption. It characterises which supports leak through vanishing power sums and analyses how sparse distortions act on dual codewords. It also studies sampling methods for the mask, and states that the ciphertext-level assumption is not refuted. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show the DFV key assumption fails for full support via parity leakage, characterize support restrictions, and analyse mask sampling methods.

entry.title: Impossibility Results for Perfect Additive Randomized Encodings
entry.summary: On Perfect Additive Randomized Encodings IACR ePrint · Nov 27, 2026This paper studies Additive Randomized Encodings (AREs), which encode each input locally so that the function output can be decoded from the sum of the encodings while revealing nothing else about the inputs. The authors show that no ARE can achieve both perfect security and perfect correctness for OR over any finite Abelian group, and likewise for XOR over Z_p with prime p>2 under a rationality assumption. They also partially rule out perfectly correct AREs for OR with imperfect security under natural restrictions, and rule out perfectly secure AREs with nontrivial correctness error over histograms, which extends to protocols in the shuffle model. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove nonexistence of perfect AREs for OR over finite Abelian groups and XOR over Z_p, with partial negative results for perfectly correct AREs.

entry.title: Near-n-bit preimage and second-preimage security of the JH hash mode
entry.summary: Near-n-Bit Preimage and Second-Preimage Security of the JH Mode IACR ePrint · Nov 27, 2026This paper revisits the JH hash mode in the ideal-permutation model, where earlier direct bounds on preimage and second-preimage resistance were only at the birthday scale. Using Menger's theorem and a potential function, the authors derive bounds that give negligible advantage for messages up to 2^64 bits within about 2^(n-2√(2n)-O(log n)) queries. For JH-512, the certificates keep preimage success below 1/2 up to 2^431 queries and second-preimage up to 2^416. A Lean 4 formalization of the proofs is included. ★★★★ Notable: In the ideal-permutation model, the authors use Menger's theorem and a potential to improve JH preimage and second-preimage bounds from birthday scale, with Lean 4 proofs.

entry.title: Extending Arithmetic Masking Security to All Finite Cyclic Groups via Fourier Analysis
entry.summary: Extending the Security of Arithmetic Masking to All Finite Cyclic Groups via Fourier Analysis IACR ePrint · Nov 27, 2026This paper studies a secret-sharing scheme in which a secret in the integers modulo N is split into k shares, and bounds how far the joint distribution of the shares' Hamming weights is from the distribution obtained when the secret is uniform. The authors prove that for every N≥2 and fixed k≥3, this total variation distance is O(n^(-k/2+5/4)) uniformly over all secrets, where n is the ceiling of log2 N. The proof uses Fourier analysis on the Boolean cube and a decomposition of the range into intervals with power-of-two lengths. The result removes the earlier requirement that the modulus be close to a power of two, while keeping the exponent of the general bound by Biswas et al. ★★★★ Notable: The authors extend arithmetic masking security bounds from near-power-of-two moduli to all finite cyclic groups via Fourier analysis on the Boolean cube.

entry.title: Exact post-quantum security analysis of Ascon authenticated encryption under nonce misuse
entry.summary: Exact Post-Quantum Security Analysis of Ascon Authenticated Encryption under Nonce Misuse IACR ePrint · Nov 27, 2026This paper studies the post-quantum security of Ascon AEAD, a lightweight authenticated encryption algorithm standardized by NIST as SP 800-232, when nonces are reused. Using the quantum random permutation model, the authors prove confidentiality and authenticity security up to min{2^(κ/2), 2^(c/3)} queries, improving the key-length dependence of a previous bound from 2^(κ/3). They also construct quantum attacks based on classical nonce-misuse attacks, showing that the bounds are tight in the exponent. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a new decomposition of Ascon AEAD, improve the key-length dependence of a prior bound, and report matching quantum attacks showing tight bounds.

entry.title: BIFOLD: Memory-Efficient Homomorphic CNN Inference over Bivariate Rings
entry.summary: BIFOLD: Memory-Efficient Homomorphic CNN Inference over Bivariate Rings IACR ePrint · Nov 26, 2026This paper addresses private convolutional neural network inference using fully homomorphic encryption, where large evaluation keys hinder practical use. It introduces an exponential bootstrapping method and low-depth functional bootstrapping for densely packed inputs, and uses a bivariate ring to enable compact plaintexts and fuse convolution into bootstrapping. On an RTX 5090 at ring degree N=2^15, ResNet-20 inference takes 127.8 ms, 2.19 times faster than the RBOOT baseline, with evaluation keys 6.1 times smaller. Seeding mask polynomials reduces the keys to 0.84 GB at 140.1 ms latency.

entry.title: Security Analysis of Homogeneous MQ-Based Post-Quantum Signatures
entry.summary: Security Analysis of Homogeneous MQ-Based Post-Quantum Signature Schemes IACR ePrint · Nov 26, 2026This paper analyzes the security of post-quantum signature schemes built on homogeneous multivariate quadratic (MQ) systems. It compares direct and target-quotient solving costs across recommended UOV, SNOVA, and QR-UOV parameter sets, and reports experimental recovery rates over a finite field. It also derives an exact recovery law in the random UOV model and finite recovery bounds.

entry.title: Elligator Prime: Injective Encoding of Elliptic Curve Points Without Torsion Assumptions
entry.summary: Elligator Prime: Injective Encodings to Elliptic Curves Without Torsion Assumptions IACR ePrint · Nov 26, 2026The paper presents Elligator Prime, a method for encoding finite-field elements as rational points on elliptic curves. Unlike earlier injective encodings, it does not require a rational torsion point of prescribed order. It replaces Skałba's equality with an odd-parity identity on four Möbius branches, and covers curves of prime order as well as several other families.

entry.title: Using Redundant PMNS Arithmetic to Reduce Side-Channel Leakage in ML-DSA
entry.summary: Exploring Redundant PMNS Arithmetic for Side-Channel Leakage Reduction in ML-DSA IACR ePrint · Nov 26, 2026This paper applies Polynomial Modular Number Systems (PMNS), previously studied for large-prime elliptic curve arithmetic, to the small modulus used by ML-DSA, a lattice-based signature scheme. The authors design a tailored PMNS instantiation for efficient modular reduction and use its redundancy to randomize intermediate values, reducing side-channel leakage without classical masking. Evaluation combines leakage detection and machine-learning profiling attacks on the Number Theoretic Transform, showing reduced first-order leakage. Cycle-accurate profiling on a RISC-V CVA6 core shows a slowdown comparable to standard countermeasures.

entry.title: Hardness Results for Decomposed Learning with Errors Problems
entry.summary: On the Hardness of Decomposed Learning with Errors Problems IACR ePrint · Nov 26, 2026This cryptography preprint strengthens the known hardness reduction for the decision version of the Decomposed Learning With Errors (LWE) problem and also gives a reduction for its search version. In both cases, the authors reduce the t-succinct LWE problem to Decomposed LWE. The earlier decision-version reduction relied on Gaussian noise flooding, which made the modulus-to-noise ratio super-polynomial in the security parameter. The new reductions hold in the polynomial regime when the number of decompositions is polynomial.

entry.title: A method for deriving inverse formulas of shift-invariant transformations using one residual variable
entry.summary: A One-Residual Procedure for Deriving Inverse Expressions of Shift-Invariant Transformations IACR ePrint · Nov 26, 2026The paper presents a one-residual procedure that derives factorized inverse expressions for a class of shift-invariant transformations by iteratively isolating a single residual input variable and propagating the recurrence along cyclic orbits. For transformations with one nonlinear product term that meet explicit cancellation conditions, the authors prove a necessary and sufficient arithmetic criterion for bijectivity. Applying this criterion, they construct degree-t permutations that attain a known inverse-degree bound.

entry.title: Rotten CHERIs: a study of whether hardware memory protection on RISC-V holds up against physical fault attacks
entry.summary: Rotten CHERIs - A Comprehensive Study of Faults in CHERI RISC-V IACR ePrint · Nov 26, 2026CHERI is a hardware-based approach to preventing memory vulnerabilities. This paper presents the first fault analysis of CHERI on RISC-V systems, examining how faults affect capabilities and capability management instructions. It finds that CHERI makes meaningful fault attacks harder but does not prevent them entirely. The authors built a Spike-based fault simulator, demonstrate fault attacks that still violate CHERI's memory-safety guarantees, and discuss possible countermeasures.

entry.title: Faster post-quantum public-key PCFs for oblivious transfer
entry.summary: (Significantly) Faster Post-Quantum Public-Key PCFs for OT IACR ePrint · Nov 26, 2026This paper studies post-quantum Public-Key Pseudorandom Correlation Functions (PK-PCFs) for Oblivious Transfer (OT), which let users publish public keys so any pair can non-interactively generate many correlated strings to speed up secure computation. The authors give a new lattice-based construction that relies on roughly the same assumptions as prior work by Agrawal et al. but is built from a new blueprint using public-key algebraic homomorphic MACs. Their implementation reports throughput of about 208k OTs per second for the sender and 189k for the receiver on one thread, substantially faster than previous post-quantum constructions.

entry.title: A unified algebraic method for fast homomorphic matrix operations across encodings
entry.summary: One Algebra to Multiply Them All: Fast Homomorphic Linear Algebra in Every Encoding IACR ePrint · Nov 26, 2026The paper shows how to reduce homomorphic matrix multiplication to plaintext matrix multiplication directly in the slot encoding over the standard power-of-two CKKS ring, without changing the ciphertext ring. It uses the cyclic algebra of a cyclotomic field extension to describe endomorphisms independently of coordinates, so that choosing a basis corresponds to choosing an encoding. The framework also covers products of two encrypted matrices, with a stated count of key switchings.

entry.title: Stable Private Intersection with Consistency (SPICy): a framework that binds both parties to their committed sets
entry.summary: Stable Private Intersection with Consistency IACR ePrint · Nov 27, 2026This paper introduces SPICy, a framework for private set intersection that binds both parties to their exact committed input sets across repeated intersections. It prevents a party from omitting elements, which would otherwise cause false negatives and biased outputs. SPICy builds on MiniPSI and introduces a new primitive, the Mutual Oblivious PRF, to achieve complete input consistency with a single round of online communication. The authors report online runtime overhead of 1.7–1.9× and communication overhead of about 4.5× compared to MiniPSI for set sizes from 2⁷ to 2¹⁰.

entry.title: A randomized primality proving method generalized using twisted polynomials
entry.summary: A Generalization of A Randomized AKS-Class Primality Proving Algorithm via Twisted Polynomials IACR ePrint · Nov 27, 2026This paper extends Bernstein's combinatorial primality certificates by varying the linear factors and coefficient degree in a Kummer-type quotient ring. It separates the coefficient period from the extension degree and replaces an auxiliary factor with direct period tests. Under stated hypotheses, the results strengthen the certificate criteria, but they do not yield a smaller general complexity exponent than Bernstein's essentially quartic algorithm.

entry.title: Aggregation methods for SPoCK, a way to prove shared secret knowledge across many parties
entry.summary: Aggregation techniques for the SPoCK scheme IACR ePrint · Nov 27, 2026A prior paper formalized Specialized Proof of Confidential Knowledge (SPoCK), which lets two independent parties convince a third party they share a secret without revealing it. This work introduces Multi-SPoCK, which lets two sets of provers show they derived their proofs from the same secret, and Aggregate Multi-SPoCK, which combines proofs over multiple secrets into one. The authors give a security model and pairing-based constructions from BLS multisignatures, with security proofs under suitable computational assumptions.

entry.title: A Fast Two-Party Protocol for Securely Sampling Any Public Discrete Distribution
entry.summary: Lightning-fast Two-Party Secure Sampling Protocol for Arbitrary Public Discrete Distributions IACR ePrint · Nov 27, 2026This paper presents a two-party secure computation protocol that samples from arbitrary public discrete distributions without revealing the generated randomness. The target distribution is compiled into a representation built from table-representable mixtures and deterministic transformations, and arithmetic shares of a sample are generated from this approximation. Security is proven against a static semi-honest adversary corrupting one party. The method is evaluated on five families of discrete distributions used in randomized algorithms and differential privacy.

entry.title: "Adams Bridge is Falling Down": New Chosen-Ciphertext Side-Channel Attack on a Post-Quantum Crypto Accelerator
entry.summary: Adams Bridge is Falling Down: A New Chosen Ciphertext Side-Channel Attack on the PQC Accelerator IACR ePrint · Nov 25, 2026This paper reports new vulnerabilities in the Adams Bridge hardware accelerator, which implements ML-KEM and ML-DSA and serves as the post-quantum engine of Caliptra 2.1. The authors present the first practical key recovery attack on the released v2.0.3 ML-KEM implementation with all countermeasures enabled. They also propose a non-profiled chosen-ciphertext attack that recovers the full ML-KEM-1024 secret key using 18,580 traces in 49.5 minutes, reducing traces by at least 29.2% compared with their profiled attack. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a new non-profiled chosen-ciphertext side-channel attack, reporting the first practical key recovery on Adams Bridge ML-KEM with all countermeasures enabled.

entry.title: Nearly Optimal Lower Bounds for Pairing-Based Succinct Non-Interactive Arguments
entry.summary: (Almost) Tight Bounds for Pairing-Based SNARGs IACR ePrint · Nov 25, 2026This paper constructs a publicly verifiable succinct non-interactive argument (SNARG) for NP in the asymmetric bilinear generic group and random oracle models. At λ bits of security, a proof consists of one G1 element plus λ+o(λ) additional bits. Assuming exponentially secure pseudorandom generators and natural restrictions on setup and verification, the authors show the additional bit string cannot have length o(λ). They also present a variant of the KZG polynomial commitment scheme that saves one pairing during verification compared with standard KZG. ★★★★ Notable: The authors construct a pairing-based SNARG with near-tight proof-length bounds and a KZG variant saving one pairing.

entry.title: Constant-size identity-based linkable ring signatures using standard assumptions
entry.summary: Constant-Size Identity-Based Linkable Ring Signatures from Standard Assumptions IACR ePrint · Nov 25, 2026This paper proposes an identity-based linkable ring signature scheme whose signatures have constant size and whose security is proven in the standard model under standard assumptions. Earlier schemes of this kind were proven secure only in the random oracle model, and those with constant-size signatures also relied on non-standard assumptions. The construction is built from a constant-size hierarchical identity-based encryption scheme, adapted to a matrix-based dual-system framework. The authors prove unforgeability, linkability, and non-slanderability under the Matrix Decisional Diffie-Hellman assumption. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give a constant-size identity-based linkable ring signature in the standard model, with security proven under the MDDH assumption.

entry.title: Beyond the Input-Length Barrier: How Many AND and OT Calls Secure Two-Party Computation Needs
entry.summary: Beyond the Input-Length Barrier: AND and OT Complexity of Two-Party Computation IACR ePrint · Nov 25, 2026This paper studies how many calls to AND or Oblivious Transfer (OT) are needed to securely compute a given function between two parties. The authors prove that Inner Product, equality, and Hamming proximity require about 1.29n AND calls, and that almost every Boolean function on two n-bit inputs requires about 1.26n OT calls. They also give a perfectly secure randomized protocol for Inner Product using about 1.71n AND calls. Finally, they show randomized protocols can be derandomized in parallel without increasing the number of AND calls. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give explicit AND and OT call lower bounds beyond input length, plus an improved randomized AND protocol for Inner Product.

entry.title: When Verification Leaks: Fixing Verifiable PIR That Reveals Queries
entry.summary: When Verification Leaks: Breaking and Repairing Verifiable PIR with Small Client Storage IACR ePrint · Nov 25, 2026Verifiable private information retrieval (vPIR) lets a client privately fetch a database entry and check the server's answer. A 2026 IEEE S&P scheme reduces client storage by delegating hint computations to the server with homomorphic encryption, claiming that accepting or rejecting responses leaks nothing about the query. This paper refutes that claim with two selective-failure attacks by a malicious server. It then repairs the scheme by requiring the server to prove that returned ciphertexts are correct before decryption, preserving query privacy and answer correctness without large client storage. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report a selective-failure attack on a small-storage vPIR scheme and a proof-based repair that removes the leak.

entry.title: Quorus 2.0: A Practical, Scalable Threshold Signature Scheme for the NIST-Standardized ML-DSA
entry.summary: Quorus 2.0: Practical and Scalable Threshold Signature Scheme for NIST-Standardized ML-DSA IACR ePrint · Nov 25, 2026This paper presents a threshold signature scheme for ML-DSA, the post-quantum signature algorithm standardized by NIST as FIPS 204, allowing a group of signers, none of whom holds the full key, to jointly produce signatures that pass the unmodified standard verification. The authors note limitations of prior approaches, including party-count limits, many online rounds, and reliance on added noise or extra assumptions. They prove that transcripts of rejected signing attempts can be simulated statistically without noise or additional assumptions. Building on this, they construct an efficient protocol using only arithmetic modulo ML-DSA's native modulus q. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove rejected ML-DSA transcripts can be simulated statistically without noise or extra assumptions, and build a threshold scheme using only arithmetic modulo q that scales to any n.

entry.title: Forging Encrypted Checksums in Verifiable FHE: A Cryptanalysis of DataSeal
entry.summary: Forging Encrypted Linear Checksums in Verifiable FHE: A Cryptanalysis of DataSeal IACR ePrint · Nov 25, 2026This paper examines DataSeal (IEEE S&P 2025), a scheme that gives a fully homomorphic encryption evaluator encrypted secret linear checksums. It shows attacks that let an incorrect output pass verification, including forgeries against each of its two matrix checks. The authors also analyze a repair that adds independent checksum rows and run SEAL/BGV experiments to test the feasibility of the attacks and selected countermeasures. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors present forgeries against DataSeal's linear checksums and analyze multi-row repairs; they report executing attacks on SEAL/BGV and changing MNIST predictions.

entry.title: MechCrypto: AI-assisted cryptanalysis of first-round NGCC candidate algorithms
entry.summary: MechCrypto: Agent-Assisted Cryptanalysis of the First-Round NGCC Candidates IACR ePrint · Nov 26, 2026This paper presents MechCrypto, a cryptanalysis research agent built on a persistent graph-structured framework, combining task contracts, cross-artifact provenance, on-demand cryptographic knowledge packs, and an independent verification gate. The authors blindly evaluated it on all 119 first-round candidates of the NGCC program, covering signatures, key encapsulation, key exchange, and hash functions, without access to existing attack reports. The campaign produced 115 comparable principal results, including 23 Critical findings. The authors report higher severity ratings than the public results on several candidates. ★★★★ Notable: The authors apply a persistent graph-structured agent to cryptanalysis with an independent verification gate; the abstract reports 115 principal results across 119 NGCC candidates, 23 rated Critical.

entry.title: Computational Bernoulli Smoothing and Worst-Case Errors in LPN Reductions
entry.summary: Computational Bernoulli Smoothing and Worst-Case Errors in LPN Reductions IACR ePrint · Nov 26, 2026This paper studies Learning Parity with Noise (LPN), a central problem in post-quantum cryptography, and improves a worst-case hardness reduction by Aggarwal et al. (TCC 2026) for the low-noise regime. The authors remove two restrictions of that result: Bernoulli error for the decoding alternative and fixed-weight noise for the dual distinguishing alternative. Their main tool is a computational Bernoulli perturbation bound for finite groups, which states that if a perturbed distribution is ε-pseudorandom, the original is ε/(1-2β)-pseudorandom, and this bound is shown to be tight. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give a computational Bernoulli perturbation bound for finite groups, removing prior noise-distribution restrictions in LPN reductions, with a tight bound.

entry.title: Reducing Toffoli Gate Counts in In-Place S-Box Circuits
entry.summary: Minimizing Toffoli Gate Counts in In-Place S-Box Implementations IACR ePrint · Nov 24, 2026This paper studies ancilla-free in-place quantum circuits for the Ascon S-box and the 5-bit Keccak χ5 mapping. The authors develop a complete synthesis method that treats NOT and CNOT gates as affine operations and prunes the search space using a canonical state representation and a proven lower bound. They determine that the minimum Toffoli count for both functions is seven, with a minimum Toffoli depth of seven. They also present optimized Clifford+T implementations of these circuits.

entry.title: Unmasking Glitches: How Timing Shifts Make Secure Hardware Leak
entry.summary: Unmasking Glitches: Why Secure Hardware Gadgets Still Leak IACR ePrint · Nov 25, 2026This paper examines why masked hardware gadgets with formal probing security can still leak data-dependent information through glitches. The authors perform gate-level evaluations of three masked AND gadgets (HPC2, HPC3, COMAR) under input transitions, clock skew, and temperature variation. They find these factors all shift signal arrival times, altering glitch behavior and producing reproducible sensitive-value-dependent patterns. Simulation results are supported by post-silicon optical probing measurements.

entry.title: FLoRA: LoRA Fine-Tuning of Language Models under Fully Homomorphic Encryption
entry.summary: FLoRA: LoRA Fine-Tuning for Language Models under Fully Homomorphic Encryption IACR ePrint · Nov 25, 2026This paper presents FLoRA, a framework that uses Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) to train LoRA adapters and run inference on encrypted language model data. The goal is to keep sensitive prompts and datasets confidential even when processed on untrusted cloud infrastructure. The authors evaluate FLoRA by fine-tuning the SmolLM2-360M model on the SST-2 dataset, reporting stable performance and efficiency.

entry.title: Security bounds for the FALCON signature scheme in the quantum random oracle model
entry.summary: Bounding the security of the FALCON signature scheme in the quantum random oracle model IACR ePrint · Nov 25, 2026This paper examines the security of FALCON, a post-quantum digital signature scheme. Earlier work found an oversight in its published security proof, which had only been fixed in the classical random oracle model. The paper gives the first complete security proof for FALCON in the quantum random oracle model, reducing its security to the RISIS problem and the NTRU learning problem. It also provides parameter sets that meet the security levels NIST requires under this reduction.

entry.title: ClearWater: A zero-knowledge framework for embedding and verifying hardware IP watermarks
entry.summary: ClearWater: A Zero-Knowledge Local-Context Hardware IP Watermarking Framework IACR ePrint · Nov 25, 2026ClearWater embeds hardware IP watermarks during standard-cell placement in LLM-assisted design flows. It verifies detection with a zero-knowledge Groth16 proof, so the owner's key is not revealed. In the authors' testbench, routed AES, SHA-256, and ChaCha layouts kept every registered mark with no measured cell-area growth.

entry.title: Dovetail: A Group-Action Adaptor Signature Using a Two-Block Construction
entry.summary: Dovetail: Group-Action Adaptor Signatures via a Heterogeneous Two-Block Construction IACR ePrint · Nov 25, 2026This paper presents Dovetail, a group-action adaptor signature scheme built from a heterogeneous two-block construction over multiple public keys, aimed at uses such as atomic swaps and payment channels. It pairs a large non-cheating block with a small cheating block so that soundness amplification is decoupled from pre-signing search cost. The authors prove security in the classical random oracle model under the mGAIP assumption and benchmark the scheme against GATOR, Fast ORCAS and O-IAS on CSI-FiSh, LESS, MEDS and ALTEQ at the 128-bit security level.

entry.title: LUTune: Automated Lookup Table Optimization for Faster Encrypted Machine Learning Inference
entry.summary: LUTune: Automated Lookup Table Optimization for Efficient TFHE-Based ML Inference IACR ePrint · Nov 25, 2026This paper presents LUTune, a method that automatically optimizes lookup tables used for activation functions in TFHE-based encrypted machine learning inference. It reduces LUT input precision by folding tables and decomposes plaintext weights into signed digits to lower output-noise variance in dense layers, while checking the circuit failure bound under Concrete's noise model. On VGG6, it reports a 5.2× speedup and a 17.2× reduction in evaluation-key size compared with the lowest-latency Concrete ML configuration, using the same frozen weights and quantizers.

entry.title: Collision attacks on round-reduced SHA-3 using internal differentials
entry.summary: Internal Differential Collision Attacks against Round-Reduced SHA-3 IACR ePrint · Nov 25, 2026This paper studies internal differential collision attacks on round-reduced SHA-3 and several Keccak variants. The authors improve internal differential cryptanalysis with new techniques such as probabilistic Sbox linearization and conditional internal differentials. They report the best theoretical collision attacks on nine Keccak instances, with some attacks reaching more rounds than before.

entry.title: TB-IOPP: Repair-Group-Local Proof System for Tamo–Barg Codes
entry.summary: TB-IOPP: Repair-Group-Local IOPs of Proximity for Tamo–Barg Codes IACR ePrint · Nov 25, 2026This paper introduces TB-IOPP, the first interactive proof of proximity that is local to repair groups for locally recoverable Tamo–Barg codes. It delegates global proximity testing to an arbitrary Reed-Solomon backend through full-rank matrix folding, while keeping every query within one local repair group of the committed original oracle. The authors prove an anti-stitching theorem, establish round-by-round knowledge soundness, and construct a repairable proximity certificate for authenticated distributed storage.

entry.title: Anamorphic Broadcast Encryption, Revisited (hidden group messages inside ordinary ciphertexts)
entry.summary: Anamorphic Broadcast Encryption, Revisited IACR ePrint · Nov 25, 2026This paper revisits anamorphic encryption, which lets an ordinary ciphertext carry a hidden extra message, in the broadcast setting. It shows that the Dual-Regev construction of Do et al. (EUROCRYPT 2025) can be distinguished by an attack, and builds an anamorphic broadcast channel on Dual-Regev encryption that sends a common message to a fixed group in one ciphertext. The security guarantees are proved under LWE in the standard model, and the technique is applied to batched laconic encryption in registration-based encryption and to the encryption layer of Epoque. A Rust implementation demonstrates recovery of both ordinary and anamorphic messages from the same ciphertext with comparable encryption times.

entry.title: Stateful LLM Guardrails Without Surveillance Using Anonymous Risk Tokens
entry.summary: Stateful LLM Guardrails without Surveillance via Anonymous Risk Token IACR ePrint · Nov 25, 2026This paper studies how safety guardrails for large language models can remember a user's earlier messages to catch multi-turn jailbreaks without building a profile of each user. The authors show that two running averages per user are enough to detect escalating attacks better than judging each message alone. They propose anonymous risk tokens (ART), a cryptographic primitive in which the user holds these averages and the provider learns only a coarse risk level. The paper gives a provably secure construction from Pointcheval-Sanders blind signatures and zero-knowledge arguments, and a Rust prototype taking about 0.4 seconds per message per party.

entry.title: Which Pairs Belong Together? A Pair Selection Optimization for F4
entry.summary: Which Pairs Belong Together? An Optimization Approach to Pair Selection in F₄ IACR ePrint · Nov 25, 2026This paper studies how to choose critical pairs to reduce in Faugère's F4 algorithm, a standard method for computing Gröbner bases to solve multivariate quadratic (MQ) systems. The authors introduce two pair features, novelty and column growth, and formulate selection as a weighted QUBO problem. Based on the findings, they propose a coverage strategy that uses a sequential rule with a budget. On weakly overdetermined MQ instances over F31, the coverage strategy reduces total computation time, including selection, by 35% to 67% compared with the normal strategy, without extra memory, with greater gains for larger systems.

entry.title: Memory-optimized NIST post-quantum signatures for automotive ECUs
entry.summary: Resource-Aware Deployment of NIST Additional PQC Signatures on Automotive ECUs IACR ePrint · Nov 25, 2026This paper addresses how post-quantum signature algorithms from NIST's Round 3 additional track can fit into the tight RAM limits of automotive controllers such as the Infineon AURIX TC4. The authors apply software-level memory optimizations to MQOM, SDitH, MAYO, and QR-UOV and benchmark them on real automotive hardware against ML-DSA and SLH-DSA. They report that the optimized MAYO-3 performs best overall, while SLH-DSA and SDitH are judged unsuitable for on-device signing due to high execution latency.

entry.title: An end-to-end framework for threshold homomorphic encryption secure against malicious adversaries
entry.summary: End-to-End Framework for Maliciously Secure Threshold Homomorphic Encryption IACR ePrint · Nov 25, 2026This paper studies t-out-of-n threshold homomorphic encryption and its use as a maliciously secure multiparty computation protocol. The authors build an end-to-end scheme covering distributed key generation through distributed decryption and analyze its security in the universal composability framework. They also implement and benchmark the zero-knowledge arguments needed to verify well-formedness, quantifying the concrete cost of malicious security.

entry.title: Breaking the Curse of Dimensionality: Fuzzy PSI Without Extra Overhead
entry.summary: Breaking the Curse of Dimensionality: Fuzzy PSI without O((log δ)^d) Overhead IACR ePrint · Nov 24, 2026This paper presents a fuzzy private set intersection (FPSI) protocol for L∞ distance, which lets a receiver learn which sender items lie within a threshold δ of its own items without revealing other information. The protocol uses only oblivious transfer and symmetric-key operations and achieves optimal O(d log δ) fuzzy matching complexity without an extra O((log δ)^d) factor. Experiments show it outperforms state-of-the-art FPSI protocols under all tested parameters, with 1.2 to 174 times faster running time and 1.5 to 97.4 times lower communication cost. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a new ssPIT protocol that yields O(d log δ) fuzzy matching without an extra exponential factor, reporting 1.2–174× speedup and 1.5–97.4× communication reduction over prior FPSI.

entry.title: Remote fault attack on post-quantum signatures using statistical ineffective fault analysis
entry.summary: Remote Fault Attacks on PIOP-based Post-Quantum Digital Signatures using Statistical Ineffective Fault Analysis IACR ePrint · Nov 24, 2026This paper presents a remote fault attack against post-quantum digital signature schemes MQOM, FAEST and SDitH, which are based on Polynomial Interactive Oracle Proof (PIOP) protocols. The attack targets the underlying polynomials to recover the secret key and uses Statistical Ineffective Fault Analysis, demonstrated end-to-end with Rowhammer. The authors claim it is the first remote attack on such a scheme that can bypass fault detection countermeasures. The paper also describes a new method to bypass address space layout randomisation and proposes countermeasures. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors apply SIFA to PIOP signatures and report an end-to-end remote Rowhammer attack recovering keys while bypassing fault detection.

entry.title: A deterministic subexponential-time algorithm for solving the discrete logarithm problem
entry.summary: A Deterministic Subexponential-time Algorithm for the Discrete Logarithm Problem IACR ePrint · Nov 24, 2026This paper presents a deterministic algorithm for the discrete logarithm problem on prime-order elliptic curves over prime fields and in the multiplicative group of prime fields. Under the assumption stated by the authors, it runs in worst-case time p^{o(1)} and uses no random bits. The proof combines a deterministic construction of small affine-interval factor bases with a terminal-preserving partial contraction procedure. ★★★★ Notable: The authors claim a deterministic subexponential discrete logarithm algorithm under an assumed external construction, a striking result whose reliance on that assumption is not checkable from the abst

entry.title: EpochPIR: A Single-Server Private Retrieval Scheme with Low Communication and Near-Optimal Speed
entry.summary: EpochPIR: Low Amortized Communication PIR at Near-Optimal Throughput IACR ePrint · Nov 24, 2026This paper presents EpochPIR, a single-server private information retrieval scheme that tries to combine low communication with high server throughput. It reuses negacyclic rotations of one ring-LWE secret across several queries, letting the server precompute the needed hint products in batches, and uses a two-stage design with a SimplePIR-based column selector and an FHE row selector. Retrieving a 256-byte entry from an 8 GB database requires 74 KB of communication per query at 10.7 GB/s single-core throughput, about 77% of SimplePIR's. A communication-optimized variant uses 26 KB per query. ★★★★ Notable: The authors reuse negacyclic rotations of one RLWE secret across queries and batch hint products via 2D NTT, reporting results on an 8 GB database against SimplePIR, Spiral and ReinsPIRe.

entry.title: DC-NPSCA: Metric-learning side-channel attack for key recovery with few traces
entry.summary: DC-NPSCA: Data-Constrained Non-profiled Side-Channel Analysis using Metric Learning IACR ePrint · Nov 24, 2026This paper presents DC-NPSCA, a metric learning framework for recovering key bytes in non-profiled side-channel analysis without a profiling device or secret-dependent training labels. It builds positive and negative trace pairs from known-plaintext relationships to train a Siamese feature extractor, then ranks candidate keys by how well their hypothetical leakage labels separate the embeddings. Experiments on four ASCAD-derived datasets show that DC-NPSCA achieves higher key-byte recovery reliability than the non-profiled variant of WPSCA under the evaluated limited-trace budgets.

entry.title: Principally polarized superspecial surfaces over prime fields: counting and isogeny graphs
entry.summary: Principally Polarized Superspecial Surfaces over Prime Fields: Counts and Isogeny Graphs IACR ePrint · Nov 24, 2026This paper studies rational (ℓ,ℓ)-isogeny graphs of principally polarized abelian surfaces over the prime field F_p. Vertices are polarized F_p-isomorphism classes and edges are F_p-rational maximal isotropic subgroups. The authors give exact vertex counts and show the graph is disconnected when ℓ is odd. For ℓ=2, connectivity depends on p mod 8 and the ideal class group of Q(√-p).

entry.title: Efficient, verifiable one-shot secure aggregation that supports clients joining and leaving
entry.summary: Efficient and Verifiable One-Shot Secure Aggregation with Dynamic Client Participation IACR ePrint · Nov 24, 2026This paper proposes OSA, a one-shot secure aggregation protocol for federated learning that supports dynamic client participation and is secure against a malicious server under the RLWE assumption. It also presents VOSA, an extension that lets an independent verifier check that the server's reported aggregate is correct. The authors compare both protocols with existing one-shot schemes and with the mPVAS aggregate signature scheme, reporting reduced computation and communication costs.

entry.title: Automated checking of masked circuit parts against glitch and transition leaks
entry.summary: Automated Verification of Glitch- and Transition-Robust Composable Masked Circuits via Logic Simulations IACR ePrint · Nov 24, 2026This paper presents an automated procedure for checking whether masking gadgets, the building blocks used to protect circuits from power analysis attacks, satisfy the O-PINI security notion. O-PINI covers joint leakages caused by both glitches and signal transitions, which existing automated tools for PINI-based verification did not address. The paper also provides an analysis report covering gadgets found in the literature.

entry.title: Beskar: efficient threshold ML-DSA using preprocessed rejection sampling
entry.summary: Beskar: Efficient Threshold ML-DSA via Preprocessed Rejection Sampling IACR ePrint · Nov 24, 2026This paper presents Beskar, a protocol that lets several parties jointly produce standard ML-DSA signatures without reconstructing the signing key, secure against malicious adversaries in the honest-majority setting. Building on Quorus, it cuts online signing from sixteen rounds to three and reduces online communication by about a factor of ten. The main technique moves most rejection-sampling computation into preprocessing and combines the remaining checks with signature release. A five-party threshold signing attempt runs in under 700 ms in a high-latency setting.

entry.title: A Full-Round Attack on the CRAFT Block Cipher
entry.summary: CRAFTing an Attack on the Full-Round CRAFT IACR ePrint · Nov 24, 2026CRAFT is a 64-bit block, 128-bit key tweakable block cipher proposed in 2019. This paper presents the first full-round attack on CRAFT in the single-key model, using a dissection approach based on the decomposition of the cipher into two parts with minimal mixing. The attack breaks all 32 rounds in 2^121 time and 2^120 memory with 3 known plaintexts. It also extends to 36 rounds with 2^126 time and 2^124 memory.

entry.title: THEMIS: A Co-Designed System for Encrypted Transformer Inference
entry.summary: THEMIS: Non-Interactive Secure Transformer Inference via Level Scheduling and Kernel Optimization IACR ePrint · Sep 29, 2026This paper presents THEMIS, a system for Transformer inference under fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) that co-designs stages around depth budgets and modulus-chain placement. It reports speedups over MOAI and Euston for matrix multiplications and attention, and a faster, higher-precision softmax compared with THOR. On a CPU, BERT-base inference takes 400.06 amortized seconds per input, with GLUE accuracy comparable to plaintext.

entry.title: Recovering the full structure of linearized Reed-Solomon codes
entry.summary: Full Structure Recovery of Linearized Reed-Solomon Codes arXiv · Nov 26, 2026This paper studies the structure of linearized Reed-Solomon (LRS) codes, which are optimal sum-rank-metric codes generalizing Reed-Solomon and Gabidulin codes. The authors propose a polynomial-time procedure that recovers the full structure of an LRS code from only an arbitrary generator matrix. The results show that, like Hamming and rank-metric codes, LRS codes cannot be used directly in McEliece-like encryption. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors give a polynomial-time full structure recovery of LRS codes from any generator matrix, combining Overbeck-type attacks with shortening, ruling out direct McEliece-style use.

entry.title: Known-design attacks on LLM watermarks, and a sentence-keyed defense
entry.summary: Know the Design, Pick the Attack: Sentence-Keyed Watermarks for LLMs arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper studies watermarks that let a language model's provider recognise text the model wrote. It considers an attacker who reads the published watermark design and chooses between erasing hard-to-learn watermarks and forging ones that survive rewording. The authors propose KeyedLex, which takes its secret key from the grammar of the previous sentence, a feature rewording changes little, and whose detector need not recover the key exactly. They report that it outperforms the compared watermarks on both models tested. ★★★★ Notable: The authors use the previous sentence's grammar as a key against combined rewording and forgery attacks; the abstract reports outperforming compared watermarks on two models.

entry.title: AgentLens: Graph-guided security auditing framework for LLM-based agents
entry.summary: AgentLens: Graph-guided Security Auditing for LLM-based Agents arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper presents AgentLens, a framework for systematically auditing security in LLM-based agents before deployment. It builds an Audit Knowledge Graph from the agent's implementation, component interactions, and built-in defenses, then derives attack paths and generates validation payloads tested in multi-turn scenarios. Across five popular agent applications, AgentLens found 44 vulnerabilities, all triggered during execution, detecting 3.67 times more than the prior approach AgentFuzz. Twelve of the reported issues have been assigned CVE IDs. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose an audit knowledge graph guiding attack-path validation, reporting 44 vulnerabilities across five popular agents, 3.67 times AgentFuzz.

entry.title: Survey: Federated Learning When Clients Cannot Train, Delegated FL for IoT
entry.summary: SoK: When FL Clients Cannot Train -- Delegated Federated Learning for IoT arXiv · Nov 26, 2026This paper systematizes delegated federated learning, in which resource-constrained IoT devices hand part or all of their training to more capable parties. It proposes a framework that evaluates delegate-view privacy, delegated attribution, and constrained-owner feasibility over the same delegated transition, and audits 29 systems. Two Raspberry Pi studies show that individually established guarantees do not necessarily compose into a single end-to-end claim.

entry.title: A survey of security, privacy, and ethical risks of large language models in telecommunications
entry.summary: A Survey of Security, Privacy, and Ethics of Large Language Models in Telecom arXiv · Nov 26, 2026This survey reviews the risks and safeguards of using large language models in telecom settings. It introduces a telecom-specific taxonomy that links privacy, security, and ethics to concrete use cases. The paper also outlines open challenges, including longitudinal data privacy, cross-border compliance, and scalable guardrails.

entry.title: Model Weights, Airlocks and Sandboxes: A Call for Validating EDPB Re-identification Tests
entry.summary: Model Weights, Airlocks and Sandboxes: A Call for Technical Validation of Re-identification Tests under the EDPB Anonymisation Guidelines arXiv · Nov 26, 2026This paper examines the EDPB's Guidelines 02/2026 on anonymisation, published for consultation in July 2026, which bring AI models into scope and call for re-identification testing without specifying how such tests should be designed or validated. The authors propose a framework based on a secure processing environment with output review before release (an airlock), and distinguish forms of release and three types of evidence: formal, empirical and indirect. They analyse technical issues in three settings: model weight release, airlock review and regulatory sandboxes. They call for re-identification tests to be validated as measurement methods, with stated detection limits, bias and uncertainty.

entry.title: Making Attackers Pay More: Stateful Deception as a Cost-Exchange Method for AI-Era Cyber Defense
entry.summary: Make the Adversary Spend More: Stateful Deception as a Cost-Exchange Primitive for AI-Era Cyber Defense arXiv · Nov 26, 2026This paper argues that cyber deception should be judged by the cost exchange it imposes rather than by realism or detection, and proposes persistent, adversary-specific state as the key mechanism. It defines a Deception Exchange Rate (DER) relating adversary effort to defender resources and evaluates the defender side in an SSH honeypot combining Cowrie with a local language model. According to the paper, across five open-weight models, deterministic-layer and prompt optimizations reduced per-session defender cost by about 63% compared with a naive all-LLM decoy.

entry.title: Distance from the Truth: Why Fragmented Merchant Underwriting Misses Risk and How Source-Attributable Evidence Helps
entry.summary: Distance from the Truth: Why Fragmented Merchant Underwriting Misses Risk, and What Source-Attributable Evidence Changes arXiv · Nov 26, 2026This paper argues that merchant underwriting becomes vulnerable when evidence is assessed without visibility into its source, freshness, and relationship to the applicant. It describes three failure modes: distance from the source, the correlation gap among related parties, and treating past verification as current eligibility. The authors propose a unified evidence record built on provenance, correlation, and persistence, keeping evidence validation, identity verification, authority, and risk judgment separate. The proposed controls, scenarios, and 90-day pilot measures are presented as proposals, not observed production results.

entry.title: BridgeHammer: A Rowhammer Backdoor Attack on Deep Learning Models Using CPU-iGPU Shared Memory
entry.summary: BridgeHammer: DNN Backdoor Attack via CPU-iGPU Shared-memory Rowhammer arXiv · Nov 26, 2026This paper presents BridgeHammer, a backdoor attack that uses Rowhammer to corrupt memory shared between a CPU and an integrated GPU, altering deep learning model weights before iGPU inference. The attack places target weights in vulnerable memory and injects bit flips before inference. Tested on an Intel CPU-iGPU platform with OpenVINO across six ResNet, VGG, and precision configurations, it averaged an 88.9% attack success rate and 86.3% clean accuracy, highlighting a memory integrity vulnerability in heterogeneous systems.

entry.title: From Models to Services: A Systematic Review of Security Assurance for Model-as-a-Service
entry.summary: From Models to Services: Systematizing Security Assurance for Model-as-a-Service arXiv · Nov 26, 2026Large language models are mostly delivered as cloud services, where different parties' assets share one pipeline, yet security research on them is spread across fields with different threat models. This paper reviews the field from a service perspective, breaking Model-as-a-Service into a five-layer stack and five trust boundaries. It codes 120 studies and evaluates 50 defenses against a common set of criteria. The review finds that 44.2% of studies focus on behavioral integrity, while service integrity, availability and cost, and accountability together account for only 13.3%.

entry.title: Using Orbital Position as Identity to Re-authenticate Satellite Laser Links After Total Key Compromise
entry.summary: Fuel as Identity: Authenticating Inter-Satellite Laser Links after Total Key Compromise arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper addresses how low Earth orbit satellites can re-authenticate their optical inter-satellite links after all their keys are compromised, where existing rekeying and post-compromise methods fail. It proposes using the satellite's orbit as a trust anchor and formalizes a position-gated attacker who must continuously thrust to block the beam. The authors prove a tight lower bound on the delta-v needed for an impostor on a shared circular orbit. They present OrbitLock, a history-chained protocol combining this position gate with ML-KEM, which retroactively authenticates earlier keys once the chain outlasts an impostor's propellant.

entry.title: Attacks that corrupt privacy-protected dynamic graph analysis by injecting fake data
entry.summary: Poisoning Attacks to Local Differential Privacy Protocols for Dynamic Graphs arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper studies how malicious data injection can poison dynamic graph analysis protocols that use local differential privacy to protect user data. It introduces an absolute gain metric to measure the cumulative deviation of graph statistics before and after attacks, and builds a framework covering target node selection, dynamic fake node scheduling, and fake edge injection. The authors propose a temporal enhanced attack (TEA) strategy and compare it with equal-scale and random-scale baselines. Experiments on real-world and synthetic datasets show the attacks significantly reduce the accuracy of graph metric estimates for target nodes.

entry.title: Latent-in-the-Middle: Security of Cross-Model Latent Communication in Multi-Agent Systems
entry.summary: Latent-in-the-Middle: On the Security of Cross-Model Latent Communication in Multi-Agent Systems arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper examines security risks when language models in multi-agent systems share internal KV caches through a learned cross-model mapper instead of natural-language messages. The authors introduce Chasm, a framework that analyzes attacks across the source model, the mapper, and the handoff mechanism. Experiments show such handoffs can substantially weaken safety alignment and prompt-injection defenses, and the paper proposes a lightweight target-side cache guard to mitigate these attacks.

entry.title: Training-only constrained language model for synthetic clinical patient trajectories with leak-safe calibration
entry.summary: Train-Only-Constrained LM for Synthetic Clinical Trajectories: Leak-Safe Calibration and Auditable Dynamics arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper presents a method for generating synthetic clinical time series using a compact GPT-style language model that learns co-occurrence of biomarkers via quantile tokens. Temporal direction is constrained by per-biomarker Markov transitions fit on the training data, making the dynamics auditable. A monotone quantile map is fit using training data only and applied to test severities. On a 5,000-patient simulated testbed, the model showed better distributional fidelity and co-occurrence than an empirical sampler, and a membership-inference audit gave an AUC of about 0.5, with no differential-privacy claim made.

entry.title: Testing diffusion-based cleaning of adversarial image edits on AI web agents
entry.summary: Agentic-Level Adversarial Purification: Revisiting Diffusion Purifiers on Native-Resolution Agentic Inputs arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper studies how to remove adversarial perturbations from inputs to a vision-language agent built on Qwen3-VL-8B, using diffusion purifiers applied at native resolution on multi-element pages. It shows that resizing inputs to the diffusion model's resolution, as prior purifiers do, sharply raises clean-input cost, and that the Divide-and-Conquer purifier keeps 85.0% grey-box robust accuracy on web-shop pages. The authors attribute this robustness to the global noise level and derive three requirements for defenses, releasing their evaluation protocol.

entry.title: Spoofing Wireless Sensing via Metasurface-Based Physical Deepfakes
entry.summary: Spoofing Wireless Sensing with Metasurface-based Physical Deepfakes arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper studies security risks in wireless sensing, where existing communication signals are used to capture information about a device's surroundings. The authors show that attackers can use programmable metasurfaces to control the amplitude and phase of victim wireless channels, reproducing pre-recorded genuine events at the physical layer. Unlike earlier attacks that target single channel features, this approach works regardless of the features the victim system uses. The attack is validated in a lab study on MIMO channels and with off-the-shelf Wi-Fi sensing, challenging the trustworthiness of wireless sensing. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose metasurface-based physical deepfake attacks reproducing real events at the physical layer, independent of features; validated on MIMO lab and Wi-Fi sensing.

entry.title: Practical Key Collisions for Reduced-Round AES with Fixed Plaintext
entry.summary: Practical Fixed-Plaintext Key Collisions on Reduced-Round AES IACR ePrint · Nov 24, 2026This paper studies finding different AES keys that produce the same ciphertext for a fixed all-zero plaintext, using reduced-round versions of AES. The result bears on key-committing security of AES-based authenticated encryption. The authors present practical collision attacks on 4-round AES-128, 7-round AES-256, and 6-round AES-192, the last one below the 2^64 birthday bound. They report experimental verification of all three attacks and provide a colliding key pair for each. ★★★★ Notable: The authors break fixed-plaintext non-linear cycles via linear elimination, reporting a practical one-block collision on 4-round AES-128 and attacks on 6- and 7-round variants.

entry.title: Computational Security Verification of Signal's Implementation with Owl
entry.summary: Compositional, Computational Security Verification of the Signal Implementation Under Fine-Grained Compromise with Owl IACR ePrint · Nov 24, 2026This paper extends the Owl protocol-verification framework to give computational guarantees of fine-grained secrecy properties, such as forward secrecy and post-compromise security, for key-ratchet protocols. The authors apply Owl to Signal's entire two-party messaging protocol suite, building models and proving its core security properties. Owl-generated Rust libraries interoperate with and match the performance of Signal's open-source implementations. The authors also verify Signal's existing Rust implementation against the Owl-generated specifications. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a type-based model of key derivation chains and logical queries for fine-grained secrecy, applying Owl to Signal's two-party suite and reporting computational proofs plus Rust co

entry.title: Merkle Trees Minimize Verifier Complexity in the Random Oracle Model
entry.summary: Merkle Trees Minimize Verifier Complexity in the ROM IACR ePrint · Nov 24, 2026This paper studies hash-based vector commitments, where Merkle trees have long been the most efficient construction. In a Merkle tree, a verifier opens any bit with log n hash evaluations. The authors prove that, in the random oracle model, any vector commitment with deterministic verifiers needs Ω(log n) queries, so sublogarithmic verifier complexity is impossible. High-arity Merkle trees match this lower bound up to constant factors. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors prove a tight Omega(log n) random-oracle lower bound on verifier hash queries for vector commitments, via a computational BKR-style lemma matched by high-arity Merkle trees.

entry.title: Covering sets with combinatorial designs to resist side-channel attacks
entry.summary: Non-Complete Set Coverings as Combinatorial Designs IACR ePrint · Nov 24, 2026This paper studies non-complete set coverings, which underpin threshold implementations, a masking defense against side-channel attacks, and treats them as combinatorial designs. The authors introduce incomplete coverings, a design family that includes non-complete set coverings and is closed under the dual complement operation, and they define reduced incomplete coverings. They prove analogues of classical covering results, including derived sub-coverings, a covering-number recursion, and Schönheim's bound. These results improve several lower bounds on the minimal number of blocks, and enhanced algorithms yield new coverings and upper bounds.

entry.title: CHARTS: Fast Anonymous Routing Using Random Tags and Homomorphic Sums
entry.summary: CHARTS: Compute-efficient Homomorphic Anonymous Routing with Tag Sums IACR ePrint · Nov 24, 2026This paper presents CHARTS, an anonymous routing protocol that hides which sender communicates with which receiver. Instead of obliviously permuting encrypted messages, senders attach random tags, and a router uses multiparty homomorphic encryption to recover the messages as an unordered multiset. The authors prove simulation-based security against static semi-honest adversaries. Their Go and Lattigo implementation processes a batch of 128 messages in about 260 ms of router computation, over 35,000 times faster than sPAR with its published parameters.

entry.title: Consensus that works regardless of network timing or failure type
entry.summary: Fault- and Network-Agnostic Agreement IACR ePrint · Nov 24, 2026This paper studies the consensus problem in distributed systems, where protocols usually assume a fixed timing model and fault type. The authors extend the idea of network-agnostic protocols to protocols that do not depend on either the network model or the kind of faults. They establish tight feasibility conditions for an agreement problem across 15 pairs of classical models. The paper also compares the costs and benefits of these agnostic protocols with classical and mixed fault-tolerant ones.

entry.title: FAEST on GPUs: Speeding Up Field Multiplication for Post-Quantum Signatures
entry.summary: GPU Optimization of QuickSilver Proving and Verification in FAEST v3 IACR ePrint · Oct 15, 2026This paper presents an NVIDIA GPU implementation of the FAEST post-quantum signature scheme, focusing on field multiplication in QuickSilver as the main cost. The authors use PTX clmad for native carry-less arithmetic and Karatsuba to reduce limb products. Reported results include 26.6x throughput over the software-multiplication build for the field-multiplication-heavy kernel of 256-bit standard OWFProve, and 2.9x to 3.1x for full 256-bit OWFProve.

entry.title: FlashProve-Next: Verifiable Inference for Production LLM APIs
entry.summary: FlashProve-Next: Verifiable Inference for Production LLM APIs arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper presents FlashProve-Next, which produces zero-knowledge-masked proofs for individual responses from closed-weight LLM APIs, letting clients verify that the advertised model, precision, and reasoning budget were used. The method works without modifying native serving and without revealing weights, hidden prompts, or activations. The paper reports Lean 4 mechanized soundness proofs and proving and verification timings on Qwen3 models. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose zero-knowledge-masked proofs for LLM API responses without changing native serving, mechanized in Lean 4 and tested on Qwen3 models.

entry.title: Node-private graph algorithms via stable degree-bounded projections
entry.summary: Node Differential Privacy via Node-Stable Graph Projections arXiv · Nov 25, 2026The paper introduces two tools for designing node-differentially private algorithms on graph data. The first is a randomized, nearly linear time graph projection that leaves graphs of maximum degree D unchanged, maps other graphs to subgraphs of maximum degree about D, and is stable under changing one node. The second is a deterministic nearly linear time Lipschitz extension for total edge weight on bounded-weight graphs. The authors also show how to apply these methods to high-dimensional vector summation and gradient descent. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give a nearly linear time node-stable graph projection and a deterministic Lipschitz extension, applying them to node-private vector summation and gradient descent.

entry.title: Small Leaks Sink Great Ships: Automated Analysis of Low-Entropy Key Protocols
entry.summary: Small Leaks Sink Great Ships: Automated Analysis of Protocols That Tolerate Low-Entropy Keys arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper presents a protocol-agnostic, automated symbolic method for analyzing protocols such as WPA2-PSK, BLE, and Bluetooth Classic that tolerate low-entropy keys, implemented as EntropyVerif, an extension of Tamarin. Using the tool, the authors rediscover the PMKID, KNOB, and Method Confusion attacks. They also report a new attack on Bluetooth Classic, the Unilateral Multi-Downgrade (UMD) attack, which reduces session-key recovery cost for devices using 128-bit keys from 2^128 to n·2^(128/n). ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a protocol-agnostic automated symbolic method for low-entropy keys and report a new BC downgrade attack reducing key recovery cost.

entry.title: PRECEPT: Coding Agents Learning to Stay Secure Across Sessions
entry.summary: PRECEPT: Security Self-Improvement of Coding Agents via Evolving Principles arXiv · Nov 25, 2026The paper finds that AI coding agents can fix a security vulnerability when shown the failing test, yet often reintroduce the same vulnerability class in later sessions, at about the same rate as agents that never saw it. Neither storing the repair nor giving general secure coding principles closed this gap. The authors present PRECEPT, a library that starts from authoritative secure coding principles and revises them using the agent's own failures, keeping only revisions that improve security without substantially hurting functional success. On task families unseen during evolution, its weakest agent reached 97.1% secure working code, above the strongest unaided agent (81.9%) and the strongest baseline (87.7%). ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce security self-improvement and an evolving principle library that retains fixes across sessions, reporting comparisons over 14 task sequences and unseen task families.

entry.title: Merkle Trees Minimize Verifier Complexity in the Random Oracle Model
entry.summary: Merkle Trees Minimize Verifier Complexity in the ROM arXiv · Nov 25, 2026The paper studies hash-based vector commitments, where a verifier opens a bit using hash evaluations. It proves that in the random oracle model, any such scheme with deterministic verifiers needs a logarithmic number of hash queries, so sublogarithmic verifier complexity is impossible. High-arity Merkle trees match this bound up to constant factors. The proof relies on a disjoint product lemma, a computational analog of the BKR inequality. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors prove a tight Ω(log n) verifier query lower bound for vector commitments in the random oracle model, matched by high-arity Merkle trees, via a disjoint product lemma.

entry.title: A benchmark testing AI models' ability to find new security flaws in Windows kernel binaries.
entry.summary: Benchmarking Open-Ended Vulnerability Discovery in Windows Kernel Binaries arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper introduces DeepBinary, the first comprehensive benchmark for open-ended vulnerability discovery in closed-source Windows kernel binaries. Agents analyze target binaries using a disassembler and kernel debugger in network-isolated virtual machines, reporting each vulnerability with a crashing proof of concept. Across 12 target binaries, the evaluated models and coding agents discovered over 200 vulnerabilities, including 146 distinct previously unknown ones. ★★★★ Notable: The authors present the first open-ended vulnerability discovery benchmark for Windows kernel binaries, reporting over 200 findings on 12 binaries, including 146 unknown ones.

entry.title: WADJET: Authorizing and Dispatching Whole Jobs to Keep FPGA Accelerator Execution Trustworthy
entry.summary: WADJET: Whole-Job Authorization and Dispatch for Job Execution Trust on FPGA System-on-Chip Accelerators arXiv · Nov 25, 2026The paper presents WADJET, an FPGA logic gate that combines exclusive access to an accelerator, whole-job verification before any release, and a record of used approvals. A separate authority encrypts and authenticates each approved job with a sequence number using Ascon-AEAD128, and the gate accepts only newer sequence numbers and writes the registers of an unmodified accelerator itself. On a Zynq-7020 running a language model, it released all 21,000 approved jobs and none of 14,700 altered or repeated jobs. It uses about a third of the lookup tables of ShEF's register protection and adds about ten microseconds to job startup. ★★★★ Notable: The authors merge access control, whole-job verification, and replay rejection into one FPGA hardware gate, reporting tests on Zynq-7020 with about 35,700 jobs and a comparison against ShEF.

entry.title: Anti-AI in the Wild: A measurement study of online conflict over generative AI
entry.summary: Anti-AI in the Wild: From Toxic Discourse to Action arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper presents the first measurement study of online conflict over generative AI, from toxic discourse to anti-AI actions. The authors collected 931,640 posts from 25 Reddit communities and identified 3,312 anti-AI actions. They found 30.0% of posts in conflict-focused communities are toxic, compared with 4.4% in general AI communities. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors present the first measurement of generative AI online conflict from toxic discourse to anti-AI actions, tracing tool outputs into Common Crawl and FineWeb across 931,640 posts.

entry.title: FlipVLA: Backdoor Attacks on Robot Vision-Language-Action Models via Bit Flips Alone
entry.summary: FlipVLA: Backdoor Attacks on Vision-Language-Action(VLA) Models Only Through Bit Flips arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper studies whether a backdoor triggered by objects can be inserted into vision-language-action robot models by flipping a small, fixed set of parameter bits, without retraining. The authors propose FlipVLA, a two-stage selector-amplifier method that uses existing visual features within an FC-GELU-FC structure and builds the attack under a limited modification budget. Experiments on OpenVLA-OFT and GR00T N1.7 across four LIBERO suites achieve attack success rates of 90.22% to 100%, with task success on clean scenes dropping by at most 1.5 percentage points.

entry.title: Proving FALCON's signature security in the quantum random oracle model
entry.summary: Bounding the security of the FALCON signature scheme in the quantum random oracle model arXiv · Nov 25, 2026NIST sought quantum-resistant public key schemes and standardized FALCON as one of three signature schemes. This paper gives the first complete security proof for FALCON in the quantum random oracle model (QROM). It reduces FALCON's security to the ring inhomogeneous short integer solution (RISIS) problem and the NTRU learning problem. The authors also provide parameter sets that meet NIST's required security levels under this reduction.

entry.title: Detours That Compromise Security: Keeping Protections Intact When LLM Agents Recover from Failures
entry.summary: The Detour Is the Danger: Preserving Security During LLM Agent Recovery arXiv · Nov 25, 2026The paper studies workflow security downgrade, where LLM agents that autonomously replan after tool failures run sensitive operations without meeting the original workflow's protection requirements. The authors evaluated this through fault injection in an executable MCP/Skill environment covering seven LLMs, twelve task templates, and three security-sensitive domains. They propose ARGUS, a recovery framework combining resource-bound security evidence, isolated recovery-plan validation, and execution-time enforcement. In 864 runs, ARGUS prevented all observed protection-loss events under enforcement.

entry.title: Dynamic Reasoning for Next-Gen Threat Detection: Testing LLM Triage and Reinforcement Tuning
entry.summary: Dynamic Reasoning in Next-Gen Detection and Response: An Empirical Study of LLM Triage, Reinforcement Tuning, and Adversarial Evasion arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper reports an empirical study of next-generation security detection pipelines, using 56 reproducible experiments on a simulator and four public datasets. It compares static classifiers, graph-based methods, and LLM triage agents under limited analyst attention. Results show that LLM auto-closure removes 90% of false positives but discards 31-44% of true attacks, and that GRPO tuning suppresses up to 86% of novel attacks. The authors also find that adaptive adversaries evade LLM triage more often unless a deterministic policy gate runs before model invocation.

entry.title: SecID: LLM-Guided Threat-Aware Secondary Asset Identification for Hardware Designs
