entry.summary: SecID: An LLM-Guided Framework for Threat-Aware Secondary Asset Identification with Quantitative RTL Analysis arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper presents SecID, a multi-agent framework that identifies threat-specific secondary assets, meaning internal signals that could enable compromise of primary assets, in hardware RTL designs. It combines deterministic RTL analysis, bounded dynamic evaluation, and LLM reasoning, with each decision supported by functional influence, threat features, and attack mechanisms. The authors test SecID on seven open-source SoC and IP designs, including openMSP430, NEORV32, and CV32E40P, and corroborate results through comparison with prior work, fault simulation, and formal analysis.

entry.title: Poisoning self-evolving security policies in LLM agents: an attack that makes defenses over-refuse
entry.summary: Poisoning Self-Evolving Security Policies in LLM Agents arXiv · Nov 25, 2026The paper studies how self-evolving defenses (SED) that learn security policies from observed attacks can themselves be attacked in LLM agents. Using the AgentDojo benchmark, the authors build a single prompt-injection episode that causes SED to learn an over-broad policy and refuse legitimate requests. In 10 Nemotron runs, every poisoned run over-refused at least one legitimate task while unrelated-task performance and the original defense stayed intact. Contrastive policy synthesis and an automatic broadness-check gate substantially reduce, but do not eliminate, over-refusal.

entry.title: From Conversations to Commitments: A Shared-Record Design Study for Agent-to-Business Coordination
entry.summary: From Conversations to Commitments: A Design Study of Shared Records for Agent-to-Business Coordination arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper examines how shared, attributable interaction records can support business commitments across independently operated organisations. The authors present Talea, which combines signed AT Protocol records with A2A task execution, and apply it in a design study where an airline reallocates passengers disrupted by a booking change among three competing hotels. They find that AT Protocol supports five of six coordination requirements, while record-level access and release controls need additional enforcement. The paper also states a hypothesis about decision reconstruction and recovery within one trust boundary and specifies an experiment to test it.

entry.title: RegionAlign: Rearranging Model Weight Layouts to Make Chips Easier to Break
entry.summary: RegionAlign: Manipulating Parameter Layouts for Localized Fault Injection on LLMs and VLMs arXiv · Nov 25, 2026The paper introduces RegionAlign, a method by which a malicious model provider changes only how parameters are laid out before deployment, concentrating fault-vulnerable bits into one memory region while keeping weight values and clean performance unchanged. In software experiments with matched fault budgets, flips selected within that region caused more degradation than flips under original or random layouts. An EMFI feasibility study confirms that the weights can be corrupted physically. The authors frame this as a stealthy supply-chain threat showing that layout manipulation weakens resilience to physical faults.

entry.title: Onnx2TEE: Automatically splitting AI models for protected execution on edge devices
entry.summary: Onnx2TEE: Automated Graph-Aware Model Partitioning for TEE-based Edge AI Protection arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper presents Onnx2TEE, an automated, model-independent pipeline that partitions ONNX models between normal and trusted execution environments for non-sequential feed-forward networks. It uses graph-aware segmentation to keep computational dependencies intact while reducing boundary communication and TEE-induced inference latency. Experiments on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin with an Arm TrustZone TEE show that model parameters can be concentrated in individual segments, enabling selective protection of parameter-dense components.

entry.title: Beyond the Efficiency-Efficacy Dilemma: Transferability in Adversarial Malware Detection
entry.summary: Beyond the Efficiency-Efficacy Dilemma: A Critical Analysis of Transferability in Adversarial Malware Detection arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper studies the adversarial robustness of machine learning models used for malware detection and introduces AAIE (Adversarial AI Engine), a platform for automated security stress-testing. The authors ran transfer attacks using EMBER2018 against a Random Forest target. Single-step FGSM achieved a 52.9% attack success rate, higher than the 45.2% of iterative PGD (p < 0.002). The authors attribute this to iterative attacks overfitting surrogate networks, which makes FGSM examples more transferable.

entry.title: A survey of attacks and defenses for deep face verification systems
entry.summary: A comprehensive survey of deep face verification systems adversarial attacks and defense strategies arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper is a comprehensive survey of deep face verification systems, which are widely used for identity checks and mobile payments. These systems rely on deep neural networks that can be deceived by adversarial examples, inputs that look normal to humans but mislead the models. The survey reviews recent advances in algorithm design, databases, protocols, and application scenarios. It also examines state-of-the-art methods for generating adversarial examples and the defense mechanisms developed to counter them.

entry.title: Real Library, Wrong Controller: Auditing LLM-Generated PLC Code for Vendor–Protocol Mismatches
entry.summary: Real Package, Wrong Controller: Static Auditing of Vendor--Protocol Mismatches in LLM-Generated PLC Code arXiv · Nov 24, 2026The paper examines Python code generated by language models for industrial programmable logic controllers, where imported packages may exist yet not match the declared vendor or protocol. The authors introduce Proteus-OT, a label-free static verifier that checks imports against a version-pinned graph of documented bindings. Across 883 generated scripts, 20.4% show an import-level mismatch with the declared target, a figure the authors describe as conditional on corpus metadata rather than verified intent.

entry.title: A study of unauthorized reuse of free LLM services by third-party projects
entry.summary: Demystifying Real-world LLM Service Freeloading arXiv · Nov 24, 2026Third-party projects repackage free inference from LLM web apps and dedicated clients into independent APIs, a practice the authors call LLM service freeloading (LSF). The study examines 513 open-source projects and 1,588 inference paths across 64 upstream services. Direct HTTP or WebSocket requests account for 83.2% of paths, and 19.1% use account selection or rotation. Of 62 services with available terms, 58 explicitly prohibit at least one examined practice.

entry.title: EASE-SVM: A privacy-preserving, efficient RBF kernel SVM framework for medical IoT
entry.summary: EASE-SVM: An Efficient, Accurate, and Secure RBF Kernel SVM Framework for Medical IoT IACR ePrint · Nov 23, 2026This paper proposes EASE-SVM, a framework using multi-party computation so that RBF kernel SVMs can be trained and used for inference in medical IoT without exposing raw data. For training, it uses PEGASOS's fixed-value update property to design an efficient two-party secure kernel SVM protocol, achieving a 1.22x to 7.25x speedup over Mo et al. in the iterative training phase. For inference, it introduces an RFF-based privacy-preserving method and a lightweight two-party secure cosine protocol, which is 2.21x to 2.41x faster than the cosine protocol of Guo et al.

entry.title: SinCom: shallow, narrow sinusoidal composites for fast secure activation functions
entry.summary: SinCom: Shallow-and-Narrow Sinusoidal Composites for Low\\ Constant-Round Secure Evaluation of Activation Functions IACR ePrint · Nov 23, 2026This paper addresses the cost of computing non-linear activation functions securely in privacy-preserving machine learning. It proposes SinCom, a layered composite of MPC-friendly operators with depth 2 or 3 and per-layer width 2 to 5, linked by cross-channel weight matrices so that the round count equals the depth. The authors report function-level approximation errors for GELU, SiLU, mish, and the CRAfT domain.

entry.title: Time-memory tradeoffs speed up collision attacks on step-reduced SHA-512
entry.summary: Time–Memory Tradeoffs for Message Modification in Step-Reduced SHA-512 IACR ePrint · Nov 23, 2026This paper studies collision attacks on step-reduced SHA-512, a member of the NIST SHA-2 hash family. The authors propose a coordinated front-rear time-memory tradeoff framework that avoids repeated online message-modification computations. The paper reports reduced online complexity for 36, 37, 38 and 39 step versions compared with prior attacks.

entry.title: Jacobi Signatures: One-Wayness and Collision Resistance under Public Offsets
entry.summary: Jacobi Signatures: Certified Chosen-Offset One-Wayness and Random-Offset Collision Resistance IACR ePrint · Nov 23, 2026This paper studies Jacobi signatures, vectors of quadratic characters computed from public offsets. Under the Balanced Repeated-Factor Factoring assumption for moduli N = p²q, the authors build a compressing family and prove one-wayness even when an adversary chooses certified offset tuples. They also construct a family on canonical residues with independently sampled offsets and show collision resistance with negligible additive loss.

entry.title: Study of the solving degree and complexity of Gröbner basis computation over finite fields
entry.summary: On the solving degree and complexity of Gröbner Basis computation over finite fields IACR ePrint · Nov 23, 2026This paper studies Gröbner basis computation for solving systems of multivariate polynomial equations over finite fields, a key task in algebraic cryptanalysis. The authors examine how Buchberger's criteria remove redundant pairs and prove that the solving degree of a method combining linear algebra with Buchberger's original algorithm is bounded above by the degree of regularity defined by leading forms. This gives a rigorous basis for using the degree of regularity in complexity estimates. The paper also bounds the number of pairs that must be processed, improving on previously published estimates.

entry.title: PORTA: A Tool for Systematically Finding Security Flaws in Identity Brokers
entry.summary: PORTA: Systematic Discovery of Vulnerabilities in Identity Brokers arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper examines identity brokers such as Keycloak, Vault, and Dex, which convert authentication proofs from an upstream identity provider into sessions for downstream services. The authors define invariants that brokers must uphold, and all 60 prior CVEs they examined violate at least one of them. They present PORTA, an automated tool that uses a large language model to generate API call sequences and oracle assertions based on these invariants. PORTA found 33 previously unreported vulnerabilities in seven popular open-source brokers, which the authors trace to eight recurring patterns. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors define invariants for identity brokers and use an LLM-driven tool to find 33 new vulnerabilities across seven open-source brokers.

entry.title: "I Do Intend to Deliver": Can LLMs Run a Marketplace Advance-Fee Scam?
entry.summary: "I Do Intend to Deliver": Will LLMs Run a Marketplace Advance-Fee Scam? arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper tests whether hosted large language models can carry out the "free item, just pay delivery" advance-fee scam common on buy-and-sell sites. Using ten off-the-shelf models with a plain system prompt and no jailbreak, the authors ran 1,200 conversations between model sellers and model buyers across four buyer personas. In 737 conversations (61%) the buyer paid in advance, with eight of the ten models participating in nearly every conversation at roughly 2.5 cents per payment. ★★★★ Notable: The authors simulate marketplace advance-fee scams with LLMs on both sides; they report 737 of 1,200 conversations ended with the buyer paying in advance and release the benchmark.

entry.title: C3H: Hijacking Compression-to-Consensus Criteria in Multimodal LLM Recommenders
entry.summary: C3H: Compression-to-Consensus Criteria Hijacking in Multimodal LLM Recommender Systems arXiv · Nov 25, 2026The paper argues that multimodal compression and cross-modal fusion, often seen as defenses against content manipulation in LLM-based recommenders, can instead create a compression-to-consensus bias that favors signals that stay salient and consistent across modalities. The authors introduce C3H, an inference-time attack that tailors a target item's multimodal content to match the decision criteria the recommender implicitly uses. Experiments show that C3H substantially increases target-item exposure while maintaining overall recommendation utility. ★★★★ Notable: The authors identify a compression-to-consensus bias and propose an inference-time attack that boosts target item exposure in multimodal recommenders.

entry.title: Rewriting the PHP interpreter in safe Rust with a proof of logical memory safety
entry.summary: A Star is Reborn: The PHP Interpreter Rewritten in Safe Rust arXiv · Nov 24, 2026The paper addresses the many memory-safety vulnerabilities found in PHP's C interpreter by reimplementing it in safe Rust. It introduces logical memory safety, which confines program operations to their permitted memory, and formalizes this property through an abstract PHP machine model. The authors rewrote the PHP 5.0.0 engine in Rust and formally proved that, for a core fragment of PHP, the translation establishes logical memory safety. The Rust version matches the C implementation on functionality tests and evaluated applications, with an average runtime overhead of about 15%. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors formalize logical memory safety via an abstract PHP machine, prove refinement for a core fragment, and report results on 173 vulnerabilities with about 15% overhead.

entry.title: When permission replies rewrite the agent's rules: how a single approval can disable coding-agent safeguards
entry.summary: When Answering Is Administering: Permission Replies That Rewrite Coding-Agent Policy arXiv · Nov 24, 2026The paper shows that coding agents let plugins and remote services answer permission prompts, and that checking each answer separately fails over a whole session. One answer can rewrite the policy used for all later answers, for example by deleting a deny rule that protects secrets. The authors prove two tight bounds on what safe delegation requires and confirm their predictions across thirteen permission designs in ten agent systems. Enforcing these bounds at the shared update step blocks the attack. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors show per-decision checks fail across a run and prove two tight bounds on delegated policy updates. They report validating predictions across thirteen permission designs in ten agent system

entry.title: Authorizing LLM Agents Across Context Compaction
entry.summary: LLM Agent Authorization Across Context Compaction arXiv · Nov 24, 2026The paper shows that authorizers which derive permissions from the user's request, such as Progent, fail when an agent's context is automatically compacted, because the compactor's summary is treated as the user speaking. In experiments, the derived policy admitted an attacker's account in 91% of cases when a frontier compactor's summary was used. The authors prove a bound showing that an authorizer unable to tell forged records from legitimate ones cannot separate them beyond a limit. Their fix credits only authenticated user text carried verbatim across compaction, and in 40 attacked AgentDojo episodes no attacker action completed. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show compaction summaries are mistaken for user speech, prove a tight indistinguishability bound, and propose trusting only verbatim authenticated user text.

entry.title: Fast Encrypted Fixed-Point Multiplication Without Quadratic Cost
entry.summary: Encrypted Fixed-Point Multiplication in Quasilinear Complexity arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper addresses the high computational overhead of homomorphic encryption for high-precision fixed-point arithmetic. The authors introduce focused encoding, which concentrates precision at one embedding, together with an error-shaping technique to preserve it. They present an encrypted fixed-point multiplication algorithm for the CKKS scheme and a bootstrapping method for focused encoding that aims to avoid the quadratic cost of conventional bootstrapping. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce focused encoding and error shaping, giving CKKS fixed-point multiplication in online time O(n log n) with bootstrapping.

entry.title: Bit-flip attacks on quantized neural networks without model parameters
entry.summary: Bit-Flip Attacks on Quantized Neural Networks without Knowledge of Model Parameters arXiv · Nov 24, 2026The paper shows that quantization asymmetry makes small high-precision tensors especially vulnerable to bit flips. It introduces CoarseHammer, an attack that needs no parameter values, gradients, or data, and remains effective under continued fine-tuning. Across ten models, including four large language models, median successful runs need at most 24 flips to reach chance accuracy. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show quantization asymmetry concentrates bit-flip vulnerability in small high-precision tensors and propose a parameter-free attack, reporting results on ten models and real systems.

entry.title: Can web agents still be detected? Testing bot defenses against coordinated evasion
entry.summary: Are Web Agents Still Detectable? Stress-Testing Bot Defenses with Coordinated Evasion arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper introduces DarkAgent, an autonomous web agent that hides automation traces using a modified Chromium browser and generative models producing human-like mouse and keyboard behavior. It reports an 89% page-access bypass rate on a third-party stealth benchmark, 12 percentage points above the strongest published baseline. The authors also present a benchmark measuring browser fingerprints, interaction behavior, and network activity, finding that only combining browser and behavioral changes evades all tested checks. The timing between actions is identified as a remaining signal for defenders. ★★★★ Notable: The authors combine fingerprint, automation, and behavior evasion with a new keyboard timing model, reporting 89% bypass on a third-party stealth benchmark and a multi-channel detection benchmark.

entry.title: Variance-adaptive PMW for differentially private query release
entry.summary: A Bernstein-Type Variance-Adaptive PMW Mechanism for DP Query Release arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper proposes PMW-Bernstein, a refinement of the Private Multiplicative Weights mechanism that sets its update step using the relation between the privately estimated query error and the variance under the current hypothesis. It keeps the standard PMW privacy structure of Sparse Vector screening, Gaussian measurements, and composition. A potential-based analysis yields a global weighted energy bound and a faster update regime under a Bernstein-type condition. Simulations on synthetic data show fewer updates in low-variance settings and success within the update budget in heterogeneous settings where the fixed-step baseline fails.

entry.title: SALSA: Sampling Adversarial Suffixes from Learned Distributions for Assessing LLM Safety
entry.summary: SALSA: Sampling Adversarial Suffixes from Learned Distributions for LLM Safety Assessment arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper introduces SALSA, a generative framework that learns a distribution over jailbreak suffixes from optimization-derived attack corpora, enabling efficient sampling-based attacks on large language models. On open-source targets it matches the attack success rates of state-of-the-art optimization baselines while cutting generation time per prompt from 3.46s to 0.04s. In black-box transfer it reaches 99% attack success on GPT-3.5-Turbo and 45% on GPT-4o, more than double the strongest baseline at an equal sampling budget.

entry.title: "Attestation Is All You Need": A Zero-Trust Design for Security of AI Agents on Supercomputers
entry.summary: Attestation is All You Need: Toward a Zero-Trust Architecture for HPC AI Agents arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper examines a security risk for AI agents running in high-performance computing (HPC) clusters: an authorized agent can be hijacked and used to leak sensitive data through legitimate encrypted LLM API traffic. The authors propose behavioral attestation as a runtime defense, implemented in a system called AEGIS. AEGIS compiles task-derived behavioral constraints, intercepts syscalls with eBPF, and triggers Slurm-level containment. The paper reports that AEGIS detects all four implemented attack classes with no false positives on the evaluated benign workflows.

entry.title: Reliable Distributed Runtime Verification When Evidence Is Missing
entry.summary: Sound Distributed Runtime Verification under Incomplete Evidence arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper studies how to keep distributed runtime verification sound when evidence from nodes may be delayed, lost, or suppressed. It shows that a deadline-bounded monitor cannot be sound, decisive, and available at once under adversarial evidence suppression, so it must be able to abstain. The authors distinguish missing events, detectable via sequence numbers and periodic reports, from silent streams, which require timing assumptions. They implement these mechanisms in a three-tier architecture using MQTT and NATS JetStream and evaluate them with an LLM-planned robot swarm, measuring failure modes, runtime, and communication costs.

entry.title: Fresh Keys, Stale Secrets: Numeric Leakage in Linked AI Prompts
entry.summary: Fresh Keys, Stale Secrets: Numeric Leakage across Linked LLM Prompts arXiv · Nov 25, 2026This paper studies how much confidential business numbers, such as prices, unit costs and margins, can leak when a small firm repeatedly asks a cloud language model about them using numeric disguises. The authors test an honest-but-curious provider on synthetic firms with known values, assuming it knows the disguise method, has sector statistics and can link a firm's queries. They find that after 16 linked queries with fresh secrets, margin recovery rises markedly, for example from 25.0% to 59.4% under order-preserving substitution, and reusing one secret map leaks less.

entry.title: ReQOR: Repairing Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors in LLMs via Operator-Discrepancy Subspaces
entry.summary: ReQOR: Operator-Discrepancy Subspace Repair for Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors in Large Language Models arXiv · Nov 25, 2026The paper studies quantization-conditioned backdoors (QCBs), in which large language models behave maliciously after quantization but remain benign at high precision. The authors propose ReQOR, a training-free defense that finds the dominant directions of operator discrepancies on benign calibration data and restores full-precision computation along them in closed form, forming a factorized residual adapter. Experiments on four LLMs, three PGD-based attacks, three malicious behaviors, and three quantization formats show substantial mitigation with largely preserved benign utility, and ReQOR remains effective against a non-PGD outlier-injection attack where baselines fail.

entry.title: Testing whether a sovereign open-weight LLM keeps secrets when told to
entry.summary: Red-Teaming a Sovereign LLM, Its Reasoning and Its Training Stages arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper tests whether confidentiality instructions in a system prompt can protect sensitive information in open-weight language models. The authors red-team Apertus v1.5 and five other model families across six languages and several reasoning modes, using synthetic personal records and attacks such as correction baits and verification queries. They report that Apertus 8B and 70B leaked information in 96% and 95% of correction-bait requests respectively, and that reasoning traces can expose records even when final answers do not. The authors conclude that system prompts alone cannot ensure confidentiality and call for multilingual, reasoning-aware safety evaluations.

entry.title: CAPTA: A method for identifying the LLM behind AI agents
entry.summary: CAPTA: Identifying LLMs Behind AI Agents arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper introduces CAPTA, a method inspired by CAPTCHA for identifying the large language model powering an AI agent. It presents multiple-choice questions as verification challenges and exploits differences in models' selection preferences, choosing questions based on cross-model option-generation diversity and optimizing option sets with LLM-guided search. Evaluated on 25 LLMs from 10 model families, CAPTA achieves 99.0% mean identification accuracy with only 10 questions. Across 28 combinations of four agents and seven LLMs, it reaches 99.7% mean accuracy with 30 submitted answers.

entry.title: Power side-channel evaluation of processors using multi-FPGA partitioning
entry.summary: Power Side-Channel Evaluation using Multi-FPGA Systems arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper presents Scissors, a security-aware partitioning method for multi-FPGA systems that evaluates power side-channel leakage in complex out-of-order processors before tapeout. It uses side-channel vulnerability factor (SVF) analysis to find signals correlated with the secret key, keeping them in one FPGA partition and placing other signals on the remaining FPGAs to improve leakage observability. On a two-U200 FPGA testbed, the approach reduced the traces needed for key recovery from 49,000 to 12,000 for SingleBOOM and from 111,000 to 66,000 for QuadBOOM. It also cut QuadBOOM's RTL-to-bitstream generation time by a factor of about 9.25.

entry.title: Privacy Disclosure Control Benchmark (PDC-Bench): Checking Whether LLMs Respect Limits on How Detailed Personal Information Can Be
entry.summary: Privacy Disclosure Control Benchmark (PDC-Bench): How Faithfully Do LLMs Keep Privacy Constraints on In-Context Disclosure Granularity? arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper introduces PDC-Bench, a benchmark for testing whether large language models keep to limits on how precisely personal attributes may be disclosed, formalized as a ceiling over a knowledge-graph hierarchy. It contains 16,105 samples covering geography, age, race and ethnicity, and occupation. Across eleven LLMs, 62% of constraint violations were semantic leakage, which depended more on the permitted granularity and the task's need for the attribute than on the model itself.

entry.title: Effects of Single-Bit Flips on LLMs and Backbone-Matched VLMs
entry.summary: Analyzing Single-Bit Flips on LLMs and Their Backbone-Matched VLMs arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper studies bit-flip attacks that alter stored weight bits in large language models (LLMs), which are often reused as backbones in vision-language models (VLMs). The authors adapt representative data-free and data-based bit selectors to find candidate bits, then evaluate each single-bit flip on source LLMs and at the same logical positions in backbone-matched VLMs. Results show that the impact of single-bit flips differs across selectors, and that a single flip can make a model repeatedly output the same string across different inputs.

entry.title: Degree and cost of Gröbner basis computation over finite fields
entry.summary: On the solving degree and complexity of Gröbner Basis computation over finite fields arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper studies solving systems of multivariate polynomial equations over finite fields, a central problem in algebraic cryptanalysis. The authors examine how Buchberger's criteria eliminate redundant pairs and prove that the solving degree of a Gröbner basis algorithm combining linear algebra with Buchberger's original method is bounded by the degree of regularity defined by leading forms. This gives a rigorous basis for using degree of regularity in complexity estimates. The paper also bounds the number of pairs that must be processed, improving published estimates, especially in certain parameter ranges.

entry.title: ArabFake: A multitask deep learning framework for detecting, categorizing, and assessing risk of Arabic fake news
entry.summary: ArabFake: A multitask deep learning framework for Arabic fake news Detection, Categorization, and risk prediction arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper presents ArabFake, a deep learning framework built on MARBERTv2 that performs Arabic fake news detection, content categorization, and risk assessment together. The authors created a dataset of 2,495 manually labelled news items, with labels verified by experts. The framework reports F1 scores of 94.12% for detection, 84.92% for categorization, and 88.91% for risk zone assessment. It also includes valence scoring to highlight misleading linguistic cues.

entry.title: Query-guided image minimization to limit what cloud vision-language models see
entry.summary: Query-Guided Visual Minimization for Selective Disclosure to Cloud VLMs arXiv · Nov 24, 2026Cloud-hosted vision-language models need images sent beyond the user's local trust boundary, which can expose sensitive details the query does not require. The paper introduces QGVM, a framework that locally and trustedly minimizes images, keeping query-relevant visual content while reducing unnecessary disclosure before sending the result to a black-box downstream model. Experiments report better balances between task answer correctness and privacy, including lower face re-identification and geolocation leakage, and more accurate disclosure switching across paired queries.

entry.title: Online Environment Repair for Coding Agents: Patching Exploitable Verifiers During Reinforcement Learning Training
entry.summary: Online Environment Repair for Coding Agents arXiv · Nov 24, 2026The paper addresses programmatic verifiers used to train coding agents with reinforcement learning, which can be flawed so that policies earn full reward without actually solving the task. The proposed online environment repair method leaves rewards for triggering rollouts unchanged and asynchronously patches exploited environments during training, deploying only repairs that pass three automated validation gates. Across 20 controlled GRPO experiments, cumulative reward hacking fell from 36.9% to 0.06%, and held-out Pass@8 rose from 21.7% to 46.7%.

entry.title: APQKE-DR: Entropy-Failure Analysis of a Post-Quantum Secure Channel
entry.summary: APQKE-DR: Entropy-Failure Analysis of a Post-Quantum-Initialized Ratcheted Channel arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper examines how failures in endpoint randomness threaten long-lived secure channels in embedded and cyber-physical systems. The authors introduce the Entropy Attack Suite (EAS) and use APQKE-DR, a post-quantum channel, as a case study, measuring its handshake and per-message overhead on a Raspberry Pi and integrating it with smart grid protocols. They report that if the randomness path fails or is subverted, the root key can be recovered from public transcripts. The conclusion is that secure deployment requires integrity protection along the entire entropy path, not only strong cryptographic primitives.

entry.title: When Online Adaptation of Resilience Policies Hurts: Safe Exploration and Measurement Pitfalls
entry.summary: When Online Adaptation of Resilience Policies Hurts: Safe Exploration and Measurement Pitfalls in Resilience4j arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper studies whether an online learner can tune circuit breaker, retry, and bulkhead settings in Java microservices at runtime instead of leaving them fixed. The authors present AdaptR4j, which switches Resilience4j policies in Spring Boot 3 and uses a contextual bandit driven by Prometheus signals. With a safe policy menu and safe exploration with bounded reward, it outperforms the default policy in every winnable scenario and cuts user-visible failures by up to 3.7x. The paper also reports how a unit mismatch in an earlier test harness produced misleading results.

entry.title: Choosing Better Examples for AI Security Patch Generation
entry.summary: Not Just Any Example: Security Requirements and Fix Patterns for Guiding LLM Vulnerability Repair arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper analyzes 3,816 security patches from 348 open-source repositories to identify recurring fix patterns and 12 security impact classes based on the security requirements that vulnerabilities violate. The authors use these pattern-impact associations to select repair examples for four large language models. Guided example selection raises the four-model mean pass@3 from 37.9% under zero-shot prompting to up to 49.2%, while random example selection reaches 36.9%.

entry.title: How much access, data, and compute do AI audits need?
entry.summary: Audits Need Access, Data, and Compute. But How Much? arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper examines how much model access, data, and computing power auditors need to conduct AI audits effectively. The authors propose a framework that varies these three resources and measures their joint effect on audit success across three tasks. They find that some model access is important but yields diminishing returns, and that the three resources can be substituted for one another. The paper concludes that audit governance should consider all of these dimensions of auditor authority together.

entry.title: Study of attacks that steal prompts from AI-generated videos to recreate and edit them
entry.summary: Demystifying Prompt Stealing Attacks against Synthetic Video arXiv · Oct 26, 2026This paper examines whether an attacker can obtain reusable inputs from a single public synthetic video to reconstruct and edit it without the original prompt or generator. The authors propose V-PSA, which combines a recovered caption, DDIM inversion, and Null-Text Inversion to reconstruct videos on an independent generator. On a benchmark of 12,000 video-prompt pairs, V-PSA reaches a video-to-video similarity of about 0.9, well above the roughly 0.6 of prompt-only baselines. Correction Nov 25, 2026: Marked withdrawn by its source; no longer a pick

entry.title: Deletion, Substitution, Repair and Transplant: Component Attribution in BARBICAN
entry.summary: Deletion Is Not Substitution: Component Attribution in a Layered Prompt-Injection Gateway for LLM Tool Calls arXiv · Oct 24, 2026This paper studies BARBICAN, a layered gateway that screens prompt injection for language-model tool use. It finds that an arbitration classifier received tokenizer-corrupted text for an entire evaluation, and that repairing it raised its AUC while slightly lowering system recall. The authors argue that ablation results for routed stages can only be interpreted alongside the class balance of the inputs each stage receives, and that deletion experiments should be paired with substitution experiments.

entry.title: Using LLM Agents to Find Soundness Bugs in Safe Rust Bindings
entry.summary: Agentic Discovery of Soundness Bugs in Safe Rust Bindings arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper studies whether LLM agents can audit the safe interfaces of Rust crates that wrap unsafe code such as C or C++ libraries. The authors define a taxonomy of defects, including undefined behavior, divergences from the wrapped library, and incomplete unsafe contracts, and measure audits by a closed and an open model. They present Crustify, an agentic system built on these findings, which reported 83 findings across widely used crates and the Linux kernel's Rust abstractions, with 26 fixed by maintainers. ★★★★ Notable: The authors apply LLM agents to audit safe Rust bindings, reporting 225 undefined-behavior bugs across 16 crates and 11 more in the Linux kernel.

entry.title: HDMark: A Watermark That Proves Ownership of Hyperdimensional Computing Models
entry.summary: HDMark: Holographic Multi-Bit Model Watermarking for Intellectual Property Protection in Hyperdimensional Computing arXiv · Nov 24, 2026The paper presents HDMark, the first watermarking framework built for hyperdimensional computing (HDC) models, which embeds a multi-bit owner identity into trained class prototype hypervectors. A statistical test verifies ownership, and across four datasets and three learning rules accuracy stays essentially unchanged while a 64-bit identity is verified in 99.8% of trials. The authors also identify a dimension-permutation attack specific to HDC and counter it through encoder realignment, and an FPGA implementation shows no added hardware overhead. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose the first HDC-native model watermark embedding multi-bit identities; the abstract reports experiments on four datasets and an FPGA implementation, with impact mainly on HDC edge de

entry.title: Mining root-cause analyses into priors that guide C/C++ vulnerability auditing
entry.summary: Mixed-Initiative Mining of Root-Cause Analyses into Audit Priors for C/C++ Vulnerability Hunting arXiv · Nov 24, 2026The paper derives two audit-steering priors from evidence-backed root-cause analysis reports: Occurrence Context, which indicates where to inspect first, and Vulnerability-Inducing Structural Patterns, which indicates what failure mechanisms to suspect. On 108 CVEs from Vul4C, parser-based prioritization without LLM inference outperforms generic baselines. Packaged as a dual-SKILL workflow, the priors improve function-level broad matches by 5.3 percentage points across the cohort, with larger gains on large vulnerable files.

entry.title: Harvesting Apple's Orchard: Security Analysis of On-Device CoreML Models
entry.summary: Harvesting Apple's Orchard: A Security Analysis of On-Device CoreML Models Across the Apple Ecosystem arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper presents a systematic security analysis of hundreds of on-device CoreML machine-learning models shipped across Apple's iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and tvOS platforms. The authors collected 1,137 artifacts and converted 155 previously opaque bundles into loadable form. They report findings including plaintext learned parameters, adversarial inputs that flip classifier outputs at high rates, and small weight edits that change model behavior without a runtime integrity check. Three reports sent to Apple were declined as not crossing a security boundary, so the findings are presented as robustness results. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors report the first systematic security analysis of Apple's on-device CoreML models, with large-scale adversarial evaluations across 221 model paths.

entry.title: Your bids are showing: re-identifying power plants in anonymized market data, with a differentially private alternative
entry.summary: Your bids are showing: re-identifying power plants in anonymized market data, and a differentially private alternative arXiv · Nov 24, 2026The paper tests PJM's practice of replacing generator names with codes in published offer data and finds that, when matched against public EIA and EPA records, about 25% of scorable units can be tied to their plant. It proposes a differentially private release of monthly noisy totals by fuel group and price bin, from which supply curves are derived. At epsilon=10 per unit-year, the market supply curve stays within 11% of the truth. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors show plant identities can be re-identified from masked PJM-style offer data using ERCOT ground truth, and propose a zCDP-calibrated monthly noisy release for market supply curves.

entry.title: Aftershock: Linux kernel bugs from yesterday becoming Android exploits tomorrow
entry.summary: Aftershock: Yesterday's Linux Kernel Bugs, Tomorrow's Android Exploits arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper examines how Android kernels receive upstream Linux fixes much later than conventional distributions. The authors built an automated pipeline that screens upstream patches, reproduces memory-safety vulnerabilities on Android targets, and uses an LLM agent to build local privilege escalation exploits from an untrusted app. From 152 candidate CVEs reported over 33 months, they reproduced 38 vulnerabilities and generated 17 independently verified exploits under production defenses. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors report an LLM-agent pipeline that builds Android kernel n-day privilege escalation exploits from upstream patches, tested on Pixel 9 and Pixel 10 devices.

entry.title: When successful teamwork becomes an attack route: poisoning shared memory from within a multi-agent system
entry.summary: When Successful Collaboration Becomes an Attack Surface: Insider Memory Poisoning in Multi-Agent Systems arXiv · Nov 22, 2026This paper proposes MIMPA (Multi-Agent Insider Memory Poisoning Attack), which exploits shared memory that multi-agent systems use to store successful collaboration records. A malicious agent, using only normal participation privileges, embeds a target-specific payload during an earlier task so it is kept as successful team experience. When this record is retrieved for a later task, it steers benign agents toward a designated wrong answer. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show shared collaboration memory can become a persistent insider attack channel, reporting gains over prior attacks on three benchmarks and two LLM backbones.

entry.title: MALET and Katalina: A Large-Scale macOS Malware Dataset and Static Analysis Tool
entry.summary: MALET & Katalina: A Large-Scale Dataset and Static Analysis of macOS Malware arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper presents MALET, a public dataset of 44,804 malicious macOS Mach-O binaries and 44,457 samples undetected by antivirus engines on VirusTotal, along with 25,835 high-confidence benign samples. The authors also introduce Katalina, an open-source static analysis framework for extracting macOS-specific features. The study finds that 93.0% of malicious samples are unsigned, and 28.4% of CA-signed malware (816 samples) used certificates later revoked. It also reports that antivirus detection was inconsistent for many structurally identical samples.

entry.title: Why an Oracle Alone Isn't Enough: Secure Settlement for Prediction Markets
entry.summary: The Oracle Is Not Enough: Secure Settlement for Prediction Markets arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper examines how to settle heterogeneous prediction markets correctly and efficiently at scale, since settlement determines winning outcomes and collateral allocation. The authors compare existing settlement designs and propose a layered architecture combining incentivized crowdsourcing, stake-backed voting, and selective post-settlement review. They develop a stake-backed settlement protocol and evaluate it using historical Polymarket and UMA data.

entry.title: Where Did My Tokens Go? Verifiable Token Billing for LLM Services
entry.summary: Where Did My Tokens Go? Verifiable Token Billing for LLM Services arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper addresses the problem that users of large language model services get token bills with little evidence of which calls were charged. It presents TokenProv, which uses provider-signed acceptance receipts to establish settlement coverage and verify token charges, and uses jointly signed handoffs to tie intent, dispatch, and acceptance to the same call. The authors report 94.4–107.4% of baseline throughput across five models and state that the auditor rejected all 1,600 validly signed attack queries.

entry.title: TopoCryptoEEG: A fully encrypted framework for EEG-based brainprint authentication
entry.summary: TopoCryptoEEG: End-to-End Encrypted Framework for Brainprint Authentication arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper shows that existing brainprint authentication schemes, which encrypt only extracted features, can be attacked by a compromised client that sees plaintext query features and authentication scores, allowing it to recover the registered template. The authors propose TopoCryptoEEG, a homomorphic-encryption framework in which the client encrypts preprocessed EEG data and the server performs feature extraction, template matching, and scoring on ciphertexts. Experiments on HGD and BCICIV-2a report high authentication accuracy, with homomorphic computation taking 1-2 seconds on CPUs and about 14 ms on GPUs. The method is reported to be over 18 times faster on average than the EER baseline.

entry.title: SwarmLeak: Does Teamwork Make AI Agent Privacy Attacks More Effective?
entry.summary: SwarmLeak: Does Coordination Improve Privacy Attacks on LLM Agents? arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper introduces SwarmLeak, a red-teaming dataset of 24 synthetic group-chat scenarios across healthcare, law, finance, and software engineering, where attackers pose as colleagues to extract protected data from LLM agents. It compares a single attacker with a four-attacker swarm under matched strategies and token budgets. The swarms showed no advantage, while the choice of victim model had a far larger effect on leakage, with four of five victims leaking despite explicit confidentiality policies.

entry.title: BODYBENCH: Testing Image Protections Against AI Nudification Edits
entry.summary: BODYBENCH: Evaluating Adversarial Image Defenses Against AI Nudification Inpainting arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper introduces BODYBENCH, a benchmark of 648 fully synthetic clothed adult subjects, each paired with 11 mask variants covering body, face, and context regions. It proposes three harm-aligned metrics (sexualization, naturalness, and recognizability) to judge whether an inpainted image is a successful nudification attack. The authors audit four protection methods and find protection works in only one configuration of one method, and only under exact mask alignment. They also report that PSNR is essentially uncorrelated with nudification protection.

entry.title: TACT-Bench: A Benchmark Testing Adaptive Conversational Attacks on Policy-Governed Tool-Use Agents
entry.summary: TACT-Bench: Testing Adaptive Conversational Threats against Tool-Use Agents arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper introduces TACT-Bench, a stateful safety benchmark for AI agents that use external tools, built around scenario stories, personas, manipulation tactics, and adaptive escalation. Each adversarial task targets an action the hidden policy prohibits, and tasks are paired with benign counterparts to test whether agents still complete legitimate work. The authors also propose TACT-TrustPrime, which places a benign task before an unrelated attack, and the Paired Selective Trustworthiness metric, which measures safe refusal alongside capability on matched benign tasks. Across six models, the benchmark raises attack-induced failure rates by 17.53% over four baselines, with a further 17.01% from TACT-TrustPrime, while two defenses reduce failures by only 8.35% to 9.41% on average.

entry.title: Separating Measurement Errors from Defence Failures in Split Language-Model Privacy Tests
entry.summary: Separating Measurement Failures from Defence Failures in Split Language-Model Privacy arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper retrospectively re-examines privacy evaluations of split-trained large language models across four campaigns and two scope checks on key custody and mutual-information bounds. Each recorded claim is sorted into one of five admissibility states, such as breach, non-detection, or invalid measurement. In a 19-configuration exploration, only four of 24 required probes qualified, and those probes established privacy breaches in 13 configurations. The authors argue that separating measurement failures from defence failures changes which privacy claims hold.

entry.title: SigK: A remote PPG-based key agreement scheme for mobile health devices
entry.summary: SigK: rPPG-based key agreement scheme for mHealth arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper proposes a key agreement scheme based on remote photoplethysmogram (rPPG) signals to enable secure communication between contactless medical devices. Camera-equipped devices capture rPPG signals from human faces, and the scheme uses their power spectral density and peak-to-peak intervals to agree on a key with signals synchronously collected in a Body Area Network. The authors evaluate performance on three public datasets to show feasibility and provide a security proof for the scheme.

entry.title: Open-set radio fingerprint identification combining feature fusion and Vision Transformers
entry.summary: Open-Set Radio Frequency Fingerprint Identification with Feature Fusion and Vision Transformer arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper proposes an open-set radio frequency fingerprint identification method for IoT device authentication, which uses hardware imperfections to identify devices. It jointly detects rogue devices with an autoencoder and classifies legitimate devices with a fully connected layer. Two channel-independent spectrograms with different window lengths are generated from I/Q signals, processed by two Vision Transformers, and fused by feature concatenation. On a testbed with ten legitimate and five rogue LoRa devices, the method reached 91.1% accuracy and an AUC above 0.72 at 20 to 30 dB SNR, outperforming benchmark algorithms.

entry.title: Internal inconsistencies and unresolved experimental evidence in a quantum neurosecurity framework
entry.summary: Internal inconsistencies and unresolved experimental evidence in a quantum neurosecurity framework arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper critically assesses the Quantum-Entangled Neuro-Symbolic Swarm Federation (QENSSF), a framework for privacy-preserving, AI-powered analysis of multimodal healthcare data. The authors argue that its central security theorem (Theorem 1) cannot be satisfied under the stated risk formulation and constraints, and that the proof contains calculation errors. They also note insufficient reporting of biomedical datasets and unresolved discrepancies in the hardware evaluation, which limit verification and reproducibility of the experimental claims.

entry.title: Testing AI Security Review Agents Using an Organisation's Own Vulnerability Data
entry.summary: Evaluating LLM Security Review Agents with Operationally Sourced Ground Truth arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper presents an evaluation framework that uses an organisation's own vulnerabilities from bug bounty reports, penetration tests and internal reports as ground truth for testing LLM-based security review agents. It compares GPT-5.5, Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.7 across two evaluation strategies and analyses their reasoning traces. The models show complementary strengths, and outcome-only scoring can mischaracterise their behaviour. All results come from a single organisation's codebase.

entry.title: How Small Can One Shor Run Be? Limits and Designs for secp256k1
entry.summary: How Small Can a Single Shor Run Be? Limits and Constructions for secp256k1 arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper examines how small a single run of Shor's algorithm can be when attacking the secp256k1 elliptic curve. It minimizes the spacetime volume of the largest run while recovering every key with probability at least 0.99. The best construction shrinks the largest run 3.87 times, at 8.79 times the baseline's total volume.

entry.title: Where Agent Defenses Fail: Policy Combinations and Measurement Limits
entry.summary: Where Agent Defenses Fail: A Case Study of Policy Compositions and Measurement Limits arXiv · Nov 24, 2026The paper studies coding agents that must upload reports while sandboxes block network access, and where injected instructions may leak secrets into approved requests. Using files and HTTP receipts to measure effects, the authors run several small experiments comparing restrictive sandboxing, host mediation, and output-matching checks. Some defenses reduce benign utility, while others miss value-only or encoded disclosures, revealing limits in delivery paths and measurement. The authors note these single-model, small-scale studies do not establish general resistance to attacks.

entry.title: Fingerprinting Paradox: Why Sensitivity Weakens Black-Box Model Verification
entry.summary: The Fingerprinting Paradox: Why Sensitivity Undermines Black-Box Model Integrity Verification arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper studies how to detect unauthorized changes to outsourced machine learning models using only prediction APIs. Existing methods use sensitive fingerprint queries, whose predictions change more under tampering, to verify models more efficiently. The authors show that this sensitivity can let dishonest providers recognize verification queries and selectively hide tampering. Evaluating five frameworks across multiple architectures, datasets, and adversarial settings, they find that sensitivity alone does not ensure efficient verification against adaptive malicious providers.

entry.title: Leaks by Installments: Answer Leakage Across Sessions in LLM Tutors, and a Ledger Defense
entry.summary: Leaks by Installments: Cross-Session Answer Disclosure in LLM Tutors and a Ledger-Based Defense arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper studies how AI tutors built on large language models can reveal final answers when a learner splits requests across multiple sessions, such as by reopening a session or rewording a problem. The authors propose a persistent, per-learner disclosure ledger that builds a typed solution graph for each problem and withholds a reply if its content would let the learner derive the final answer or exceed a budget. In simulations and tests with two real LLM tutors, leakage through renumbered practice variants dropped substantially while honest learners still completed most problems. The authors also report that the ledger did not reduce split requests beyond a per-session gate in the live runs.}}

entry.title: Per-Attack Blocking Hides Catalog Vulnerability in Agent Tool Manifests
entry.summary: Per-Attack Blocking Hides Catalog Vulnerability: A Weakest-Link Analysis of Tool Manifests arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper examines the safety of manifests that tell tool-using AI agents what each tool may read and where its output may go. It argues that measuring only the share of attacks blocked per attack is misleading, because a whole catalog is only as safe as its weakest source policy. Experiments on synthetic catalogs, a pilot with fifteen authoring models, and 114 real MCP tools show that catalog vulnerability rises sharply with more tools even when per-attack blocking stays high. The authors recommend reporting catalog vulnerability, sink coverage, and an effective number of independent decisions alongside per-attack blocking.

entry.title: Fast and Responsive Encrypted Computing: CKKS Functional Bootstrapping on GPUs
entry.summary: High Throughput Meets Low Latency: CKKS Functional Bootstrapping on GPUs arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper presents an optimized GPU implementation of functional (programmable) bootstrapping for the CKKS scheme in Fully Homomorphic Encryption. Functional bootstrapping refreshes a ciphertext while evaluating an arbitrary function. Earlier work showed CKKS far exceeds CGGI/DM in throughput but trails by two to three orders of magnitude in CPU latency, which this implementation aims to close. The implementation supports function evaluation over both small integers and real numbers.

entry.title: Trustworthy Edge AI: Security, Privacy, and Resilience for Distributed Intelligence
entry.summary: Trustworthy Edge AI: Security, Privacy, and Resilience for Distributed Intelligence arXiv · Nov 23, 2026This chapter explores principles and emerging research for building secure, privacy-preserving, and resilient Edge AI systems as intelligence moves from clouds to distributed devices. It analyzes how heterogeneous devices, resource limits, and dynamic networks widen the attack surface, and reviews mechanisms such as hardware-rooted trust, zero-trust models, secure communication, and attestation. Federated learning, secure aggregation, and differential privacy are presented as ways to enable collaboration without centralized data sharing, alongside fault tolerance, adversarial robustness, and adaptive orchestration. Case studies from smart cities, autonomous vehicles, healthcare, and industrial IoT illustrate practical trade-offs, and the authors advocate a holistic, cross-layer design.

entry.title: Evaluating Agent Safety in Timeout Recovery: Proposals, Effects, and Retry Instructions
entry.summary: Scoring Recovery-Time Agent Security: Proposals, Effects, and Retry Instructions arXiv · Nov 23, 2026This paper proposes an executable evaluation that separately records an agent's tool proposals, runtime decisions, and committed effects after a timed-out tool write. It compares how often agents recover validly under different task wordings and tests whether they attempt unauthorized or changed-key actions under stronger attacks. The authors report that no unsafe effects were observed in their experiments. The main contribution is a measurement design and diagnosis of availability, specification, and contract sensitivity, not a demonstrated general defense.

entry.title: Generating Attack Trees from Attack Graphs to Analyze Unobservable Targets
entry.summary: Towards Efficient Attack Tree Generation from Attack Graphs for Unobservable Target Analysis arXiv · Nov 22, 2026This paper proposes a method for generating attack trees without assuming a predefined attacker objective. It models the threat environment as a constraint-weighted graph and applies temporal reachability analysis to infer probable attacker locations from partial observations and a time budget. The approach extracts target-oriented subgraphs that keep feasible attack paths and remove irrelevant nodes. The framework is evaluated in a single office building, a multi-building industrial complex, and an IoT communication network based on the CICIoT2023 attack dataset.

entry.title: Polarization-coded exam papers and mandatory issued glasses to counter AI-glasses cheating
entry.summary: PEACE-TEST-PROTOCOL: Polarization-Keyed Examination Papers and Mandatory Issued Eyewear that Displace AI Glasses and Extend Universal Design arXiv · Nov 21, 2026The paper proposes an examination method in which candidates wear authority-issued glasses throughout the session, while question papers are printed with text encoded in the handedness of circular polarization. To the naked eye and unfiltered cameras the page looks uniformly grey, and only the issued analyzer reveals the text. Simulations analyze luminance and contrast budgets, head-tilt tolerance, and leakage under axis misregistration. All results are simulations; no prototypes or human-subject results are reported.

entry.title: Security readiness and risk-taking in electronic data exchange: general IT versus healthcare comparison
entry.summary: Information Security Risk Preparedness in Electronic Data Interchange: A Comparative Assessment of General IT and Healthcare Environments arXiv · Nov 21, 2026This study surveyed 100 professionals, split equally between general IT and healthcare EDI roles, to compare their security-control preparedness and organizational risk-taking ability. Healthcare EDI respondents reported higher preparedness and risk-taking ability, while general IT respondents reported higher threat perception. Preparedness was positively linked to risk-taking ability, and threat perception was negatively linked. Based on these findings, the authors propose an EDI Risk Management Framework covering governance, human and organizational security, technical and physical safeguards, and continuous monitoring.

entry.title: The Industrialization of Noise: Why Automated Proof-Solving Is a Dead End
entry.summary: The Industrialization of Noise: Why Automated Proof-Solving is the Same Old Dead End arXiv · Nov 20, 2026This paper revisits the 1970s argument by DeMillo, Lipton, and Perlis that mathematical proofs are products of a social process of human critique and shared understanding. It examines the October 2026 release of 722 automated manuscripts claiming solutions to 372 open problems, which it describes as industrial pollution of the mathematical ecosystem. The authors argue that separating mechanical solving from human social understanding yields sterile logical artifacts.

entry.title: Kleptographic attacks on post-quantum crypto that account for key representation
entry.summary: Representation-Aware Kleptographic Attacks on Post-Quantum Cryptography IACR ePrint · Nov 23, 2026This paper studies hidden backdoors in post-quantum cryptography implementations introduced through Algorithm Substitution Attacks, focusing on how public keys are represented. It distinguishes seed-compressed from expanded-key interfaces and presents the first key-generation backdoor targeting HQC, which uses structural similarities with BIKE decoding so that a party holding the BIKE trapdoor can recover the randomness behind the victim's HQC secret state. The paper also contrasts this with ML-DSA and analyzes remaining seed-level attack surfaces. ★★★★ Notable: The authors present the first kleptographic key-generation backdoor for HQC, using BIKE-form carriers and a conditional indistinguishability proof, plus a proof-of-concept implementation.

entry.title: Locating a Phone Photo via Moon and Star Positions with Zero-Knowledge Proofs
entry.summary: Where on Earth? Zero-Knowledge Proof of Location from a Phone Photograph of the Moon and Stars IACR ePrint · Nov 23, 2026This paper examines whether a single phone photo of the Moon and stars can serve as a privacy-preserving proof of location. It uses lunar parallax, where the Moon's apparent position against the stars shifts with the observer's location, together with capture time, a star catalogue and an ephemeris. The authors measure results from 356 captures and turn the measurement into a zero-knowledge proof that shows the location lies in a public region without revealing the position or photo. They also analyse limits, including that a photo of a screen showing a rendered sky is accepted.

entry.title: Super-multiplicativity of a noncommutative minimum and its use in quantum privacy and hypothesis testing
entry.summary: Super-Multiplicativity of the Noncommutative Minimum and Applications to Quantum Privacy and Hypothesis Testing arXiv · Nov 23, 2026The paper studies the hockey-stick divergence, a measure of distinguishability in quantum information theory, on tensor-product states. It proves that a noncommutative minimum of positive semidefinite operators is super-multiplicative, which yields a sub-additivity property of the divergence on product states. The results are applied to quantum differential privacy composition and to symmetric binary quantum hypothesis testing, including the exact prefactor of the quantum Chernoff bound. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove super-multiplicativity of the noncommutative minimum, deduce sub-additivity of the hockey-stick divergence with applications to quantum privacy and hypothesis testing, and determine

entry.title: Relative Integrity and Robustness for Prompt Injection and Enclave-Partitioned Programs
entry.summary: Relativising Integrity and Robustness: Prompt Injection and Partitioned Enclaves arXiv · Nov 23, 2026The paper introduces relative integrity (RI) and relative robustness (RR), security properties that compare a system under attack with a reference system. RI requires every behaviour under attacker influence to be one the reference can exhibit, and RR requires the same runs to reproduce both leaks and effects. The properties are applied to LLM agents under prompt injection and to C programs partitioned across SGX or TrustZone enclaves. The work is mechanised in Isabelle/HOL, with enclave code verified in C using AutoCorres2. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose relative integrity (RI) and relative robustness (RR), which they say is strictly stronger than RS and RI combined, and give proof and disproof methods for prompt injection and encl

entry.title: IDSMorph: Self-Adaptive Malicious Traffic Detection Using Consistency-Guided Dynamic Decision Boundaries
entry.summary: IDSMorph: Self-Adaptive Malicious Traffic Detection through Consistency-Guided Dynamic Decision Boundaries arXiv · Nov 23, 2026This paper presents IDSMorph, a self-adaptive system for detecting malicious network traffic based on anomalies. It builds service-specific decision boundaries using embeddings learned from flow structure consistency and service interaction consistency. The boundaries are dynamically updated with a differencing algorithm to reduce the effect of transient traffic shifts in short observation windows. Experiments report that its F1 score decreases by no more than 0.12 points across network environments, compared with an average decrease of 55.43 points for prior methods.

entry.title: ActWithin: Limiting Wrong-Payment Risk in Delegated Batch Payments
entry.summary: ActWithin: Bounding Wrong-Payment Risk in Delegated Payment Batches arXiv · Nov 22, 2026The paper studies the risk window when a delegated payment agent holds rights for conflicting revisions of a batch and cannot verify the selected revision before the execution deadline. For batches allowing any subset of up to q revisions, ActWithin converts this limit into a shared quota of q successful replacement payments and uses a dynamic program to compute its exact risk. In an exploratory setting with 16 to 64 payments and one quarter of positions revisable, it reduces aggregate risk by 16.23% to 16.88% relative to a single amount cap on adapted IBM AMLSim amounts.

entry.title: Matching Under Metric Privacy: Accurate Private-Public Point Matching While Protecting Locations
entry.summary: Matching Under Metric Privacy arXiv · Nov 24, 2026The paper studies how to represent and randomize points in d-dimensional Euclidean space so that bipartite matchings between private and public points stay accurate under metric privacy. It analyzes local mechanisms and a Gumbel matching method for cases where a trusted server receives the private points. The authors establish a tight rate of Θ(n·min{d, log n}/ε) for expected cost above the nonprivate optimum, and benchmark experiments suggest d ≈ log n as a practical transition point. ★★★★ Notable: The authors establish a tight rate Θ(n·min{d,log n}/ε) for metric-private matching and propose Gumbel matching, with upper bounds, worst-case constructions, and benchmark experiments reported.

entry.title: FATCAT: Physical fault attacks that disable chip-level model alignment
entry.summary: FATCAT: Fault Injection Attacks Targeting Chip-level Alignment arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper presents FATCAT, a physical fault-injection attack that can stop large language and vision-language models from refusing malicious prompts. It uses non-invasive electromagnetic fault injection on GPU-accelerated systems-on-chip, with a radio-frequency side-channel trigger that times the faults to the prompt prefill phase and corrupts memory transactions. The attack was tested on NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and AGX Thor with Llama 3.2 1B and Gemma 3 1B, and was also shown to cause hazardous movements in a robotic arm controlled by a SmolVLA policy. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors present the first electromagnetic fault-injection attack removing LLM refusals, reporting Jetson experiments and a robotic-arm demonstration of physical harm.

entry.title: Hidden Supply-Chain Risks in LLM Agent Skills, From Inherited Dependencies to Agent-Specific Flaws
entry.summary: Carried-Over and Agent-Native Threats in the Supply Chain of LLM Agent Skills arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper empirically studies security flaws in 48,682 agent skills on ClawHub, focusing on vulnerabilities that skill authors introduce unintentionally. It examines four risk types: dependencies, first-party code, install instructions, and credentials printed to stdout. The authors combine static analysis, manual review, sandbox execution, and tests with a live LLM agent under indirect prompt injection to check whether these flaws can actually be reached. Many skills depend on vulnerable versions at publication, yet few of those vulnerabilities are reachable from agent input, while most sampled first-party flaws were exploitable in the sandbox. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report a registry-scale study of all 48,682 ClawHub skills, testing reachability of flaws in a sandbox and with a live agent under injection.

entry.title: Studying the Detectors That Screen Agent Skill Hubs
entry.summary: Demystifying Detectors Guarding Agent Skill Hubs arXiv · Nov 24, 2026This paper presents the first systematic study of six malicious-skill detectors, four adopted by public skill hubs and two community-provided, tested on 1,477 agent skills from seven datasets. The best-performing detector still misses 4.9% of malicious skills and wrongly flags 17.8% of benign ones. The authors identify two recurring failure causes: flagging sensitive operations without considering their legitimate purpose, and recognizing threats but underrating or dismissing them. Guided by this analysis, they refined the prompts of a state-of-the-art detector, improving its mean F1 score in eight of nine evaluation settings. ★★★★ Notable: The authors systematically evaluate six skill detectors on 1477 skills, identify two failure mechanisms, and report prompt refinements improving F1 in most settings.

entry.title: SchemaCaps: How Compatible Tool Updates Quietly Expand an AI Agent's Authority
entry.summary: SchemaCaps: When a Compatible Tool Update Silently Widens an AI Agent's Authority arXiv · Nov 23, 2026This paper examines how changes to the JSON input schemas of tools used by AI agents can silently widen the agent's authority. The authors define a non-amplification property and a re-binding rule based on subschema inclusion, supported by a Coq proof, 48 regression tests, and a benchmark. In a study of 604 releases from 39 public MCP servers, they find many compatible schema changes widen authority-bearing arguments yet are re-bound without re-approval. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors define a subschema-inclusion re-binding rule for tool input schemas, with a Coq proof and a pilot on 604 releases of 39 MCP servers reporting 76 authority-widening changes.

entry.title: Tool-call smuggling: how the same JSON can yield different calls in LLM agents
entry.summary: Oops!... I Parsed It Again: Tool-Call Smuggling Against LLM Agents arXiv · Nov 23, 2026This paper studies tool-call smuggling, an attack on LLM agents where identical JSON bytes are parsed differently by the gateway, SDKs, guard, and executor. This can cause a guard to approve one call while a different call is executed and the audit log records only the approved one. The authors built a differential testing harness across 17 parser and validator configurations and demonstrated the attack on tasks from τ-bench and AgentDojo. They propose a defense that parses each call once, keeps only approved schema fields, and seals the call with its ID in transit, which stopped all 7,412 crafted inputs and every attack they built. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors turn JSON parser disagreements into tool-call smuggling, differential-testing 17 parser configurations and demonstrating attacks on τ-bench and AgentDojo tasks.

entry.title: AgentBouncer: Defending Software Engineering Agents via Dynamic System-Call Mediation
entry.summary: AgentBouncer: Defending Software Engineering Agents via Dynamic System-Call Mediation arXiv · Nov 23, 2026Software engineering agents use tools to access files and run commands, which can let attacks such as prompt injection or malicious tools trigger harmful actions. The paper presents AgentBouncer, a runtime system that intercepts the system calls agents make through tool calls and denies unsafe ones. An LLM arbiter judges each call on necessity and safety, with policy rules and caching limiting how often it is invoked. On 340 attacks and SWE-bench Verified benign tasks, the attack success rate fell from 99.41% to 10.59%, while task success was largely preserved. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors report a runtime system-call arbiter judging necessity and safety, cutting attack success to 10.59% across 340 attacks and SWE-bench Verified benign tasks.

entry.title: MirrorGuard: Defending LiDAR Against Passive Mirror Attacks
entry.summary: MirrorGuard: Defending LiDAR Perception against Passive Mirror Attacks arXiv · Nov 23, 2026Mirror-based attacks can passively redirect a car's LiDAR beams to create phantom objects, which may cause the vehicle to brake unnecessarily. The paper proposes MirrorGuard, which uses three physical cues of the reflected path (the mirror's finite aperture, its opaque surface blocking direct returns, and dimming from two reflections) to identify and remove phantom returns across multiple scans. On real-world recordings it removed 96.31% of phantom returns at 98.30% precision, leaving 99.99% of non-phantom returns untouched. In closed-loop CARLA and Autoware tests, vehicles with the defense produced no halts or crashes caused by the phantom. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a software-only defense using physical cues to remove mirror-induced phantom LiDAR returns, reporting real-recording and CARLA/Autoware closed-loop results for autonomous driving s

entry.title: CHIP: a method testing whether CLIP can rebuild images from CPU performance traces
entry.summary: CHIP: Contrastive Hardware-Image Projection. Can OpenAI CLIP Reconstruct Images from the CPU Computational Footprint? arXiv · Nov 23, 2026The paper presents CHIP, which trains a lightweight residual projector on public images to map CPU performance counter and timing measurements into the frozen OpenAI CLIP embedding space. A frozen Stable unCLIP generator then reconstructs recognizable color scenes from these projected embeddings. Evaluated on Intel Haswell and Sapphire Rapids, held-out image identification reaches 0.85 ROC AUC against a 0.50 baseline, and elapsed time alone retains the signal. Reconstructions average 1.4 times the baseline color-palette overlap and 2.5 times the baseline structural similarity. ★★★★ Notable: The authors map CPU performance counters and timing into a frozen CLIP space to reconstruct images, reporting retrieval and reconstruction results on two processors.

entry.title: Attributing security test results for LLM agents to content-free run state
entry.summary: Attributing Security Outcomes in LLM-Agent Evaluations: The Role of Content-Free State arXiv · Nov 23, 2026The paper shows that security benchmark verdicts for LLM agents can depend on run details that carry no information about the system under test, such as hash seeds, tool order, and evidence order. It introduces TARE, a framework that attributes a reported effect to the agent, attack, or defense only when the effect exceeds the influence of this content-free state. Experiments on Agent Security Bench show that changing the hash seed alters many agent verdicts and that sorting tools changes attack success rates substantially. ★★★★ Notable: The authors formalize content-free state as a decision-noninterference constraint and propose TARE, validated on ASB across seven agents and eighteen agent-defense combinations.

entry.title: Optimal private Gaussian multi-sampling: generating independent Gaussian outputs with fewer input samples under privacy
entry.summary: Optimal Private Gaussian Multi-sampling arXiv · Nov 23, 2026This paper gives polynomial-time algorithms for Gaussian multi-sampling under approximate (ε,δ)-differential privacy, with sample complexity optimal up to logarithmic factors. The main construction uses about Õ(m+d√m/ε) input samples from a d-dimensional Gaussian with unknown mean and covariance to produce m exactly independent outputs whose joint distribution is α-close in total variation to the product distribution. Compared with running a single-sampler separately on each output, which costs Õ(md/ε) samples, the method reduces the dimension-dependent cost from linear to square-root dependence on the number of outputs. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report polynomial-time Gaussian multi-sampling with square-root dependence on output count and matching lower bounds, with exactly independent outputs.

entry.title: Checking Declared AI Workloads Using GPU Power Supply Current
entry.summary: Verifying Declared AI Workloads from GPU Supply Current arXiv · Nov 23, 2026This paper examines whether an external observer can verify the work a GPU operator declares using only the GPU's supply current, without examples of prohibited workloads. The authors recorded 23.4 hours of current with a Rogowski coil across idle, training, and inference runs. A one-class model trained on declared idle and inference work flagged at least 99.9% of windows containing prohibited training, including training hidden by five evasion strategies. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report verifying declared GPU workloads from supply current alone, without prohibited examples, across 23.4 hours and five evasion strategies, relevant to compute governance.

entry.title: LODESTONE: A system that links system events to threat intelligence to build evidence-based cyber attack reports
entry.summary: LODESTONE: Linking System Events to Threat Intelligence for Evidence-Grounded Cyber Attack Investigation arXiv · Nov 23, 2026This paper presents LODESTONE, a system that aligns events observed in system provenance graphs with attack relations from cyber threat intelligence (CTI), so that attack reports can be grounded in execution evidence. It combines a CTI-driven training-data engine, an expert-verified benchmark, text and graph relevance scoring, dual-softmax retrieval, and a fine-tuned 4B-parameter language model. Evaluated on 27 expert-verified attack cases and 713 CTI articles, it reaches an 82% attack-step description score and 91% attack identification, compared with 73% and 32% using provenance alone. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report a CTI-driven training engine and LLM agent aligning provenance graphs with attack knowledge, evaluated on 27 expert-verified cases against baselines, mainly affecting cyber investig

entry.title: Unshardable Codes: Encoding Data So Single Pieces Cannot Be Censored Alone
entry.summary: Unshardable Codes arXiv · Nov 23, 2026This paper introduces a coding-theory problem motivated by censorship resistance, asking whether data pieces can be encoded jointly so that erasing any one piece destroys many others. The authors define (ℓ,s)-unshardable codes and construct linear codes achieving s=(1-ε)k with locality ℓ=O_ε(1). They also prove a bound s≤k-k/ℓ+1 for linear unshardable codes and show that any locally decodable code can be converted into an unshardable one while preserving locality. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce unshardable codes motivated by censorship resistance, construct linear codes with superregular generators, and prove a linear lower bound on s.

entry.title: FORGETMENOT: Auditing Privacy Risks of Memory in Commercial AI Agents
entry.summary: FORGETMENOT: Auditing Memory Driven Privacy Risks in Commercial AI Agents arXiv · Nov 23, 2026This paper proposes FORGETMENOT, an auditing framework for analyzing privacy risks of long-term memory in commercial AI agents, covering storage, disclosure, transparency, and deletion control. The authors collected about 3,800 multi-turn sessions across five popular agents. Results show agents store many personal attributes, including demographics, health, and sensitive details, while user-visible memory reveals about 20% fewer attributes on average.
